pages.title: Encrypted live sharing
pages.description: Share a note live through a server that stores and relays only ciphertext, names and cursors included.
pages.md:
A note you share from Lumen goes through the collab server end-to-end
encrypted. The server keeps people to their [roles](/collab/sharing/) and
holds the room's history, but it can't read the note, its comments, or
who is in it and where their cursor is.

## What the server sees

| | Encrypted in the browser | What the server holds |
|---|---|---|
| The note | Yes (AES-GCM-256, a [ciphertext transport document](/collab/encryption/)) | Envelopes `{v, iv, ct}` |
| Comment threads | Yes, the same way (`<room>~comments`) | Envelopes |
| Presence: names, colours, cursors | Yes (since plan W2.20) | `{ "e2e": "<base64>" }` per participant |
| The room key | It never leaves the link | Nothing |
| Room name, share ids, roles, expiry | No (the server needs them) | Those, in SQLite |

The room key is in the link's fragment, after the `#`
(`#room=…&password=…&share=…`). Browsers never send the fragment to a
server, and Lumen never puts the key in a request: token requests carry
the room name, the share id or owner secret, and the operator's access key.

## Sealed rooms

An encrypted client asks for its token with `e2ee: true`, and the server
**seals** the room. From then on, for good:

- an update that writes anything except ciphertext envelopes (text, a map
  entry, a nested type, an array element that isn't an envelope) is
  refused and its connection dropped, before it reaches the room;
- a presence state with any field except `e2e` is refused the same way;
- a document that isn't ciphertext-only is never written to disk.

A room that already stores readable content (an old plaintext room) is not
sealed. To run a server that takes encrypted rooms only, set
`COLLAB_REQUIRE_E2EE=1`: every room is then sealed and plaintext clients
can't write at all.

The server checks the shape. It can't tell ciphertext from other bytes
inside `ct`; what keeps `ct` unreadable is the client, which only ever
writes AES-GCM output there.

## Encrypted presence

Each participant has two awareness instances. The editor's cursors and the
peer list use the plain one, which no provider touches. The providers sync
a transport awareness where each state is the plain state sealed under the
room key. Two values are bound into the seal:

- the participant's client id (in the GCM tag), so a relay can't show one
  participant's name or cursor as someone else's;
- a counter that only goes up, so a relay can't replay an older cursor.

A state that isn't sealed, or doesn't open with the room key, is never shown.

## Sharing needs an encrypted room

The share dialog makes links only for a room with its own key, which every
new collaboration session has. For a session joined from an old link
without a key, start a new session first.

## How it's checked

`src/__tests__/collabE2eeSharing.test.ts` runs the real server and records
every WebSocket frame both ways:

- the note's text (Hebrew and English), a comment, both participants'
  names, a cursor and the room key: **0 hits** in the traffic, the stored
  states and every file in the server's data directory. The same search on
  a room that isn't encrypted does find the text, so the check can fail;
- a plaintext writer, and plaintext presence, are refused in a sealed room;
- an edit reaches the other participant in under 150 ms (p95 over 40 edits);
- a 1 MB note with 5 participants and 1,000 random edits converges with 0
  edits lost, and a sixth participant gets the same note from the server.

## Limits

- The server still sees metadata: the room name, how many people are
  connected, when they edit and how much.
- Anyone with the link has the key. Revoking a link cuts its holder off
  from the server within seconds, but a copy of the note they already have
  stays theirs.

pages.title: End-to-end encryption for collab
pages.description: Add a room password and no relay, signaling server or sync server can read your document.
pages.md:
Lumen's WebRTC mesh is unencrypted by default: peers sync the Yjs
document directly, so a signaling server that relays messages, a
persistent collab server (Hocuspocus), or anyone who joins with the room
link can read the content. Setting a **room password** switches the
room to an end-to-end encrypted transport. Document content is then
only ever readable by peers that know the password.

## Turn it on

```js
// Either:
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "open-sesame-12345");

// Or append to the share link:
//   #room=lumen-bright-river-77&password=open-sesame-12345
```

Every peer in the room must use the same password. A peer with the
wrong password can still connect, but it only receives ciphertext it
can't decrypt. Nothing is applied to its document, and it sees a
"Can't decrypt this room" error.

> Putting the password in the URL hash keeps it out of HTTP requests
> (browsers never send the `#fragment`), but it still lands in browser
> history and anywhere you paste the link. For anything sensitive,
> share the room link and the password through different channels.

## How it works

Each peer keeps **two** Yjs documents:

| Document | Contents | Attached to the network? |
|---|---|---|
| Plaintext doc | Text, comments, everything the editor shows | **No.** It stays in the tab. |
| Transport doc | One append-only `Y.Array` of ciphertext envelopes | Yes (y-webrtc, and the persistent server if configured) |

1. **Key derivation:** PBKDF2-SHA-256, 200 000 iterations, salt
   `lumen.collab.v2|<room name>`. The same password in two different
   rooms gives two unrelated keys.
2. **Outbound:** each local edit to the plaintext doc produces a Yjs
   update. Edits made in the same tick are merged into one update,
   encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a fresh random 12-byte IV, and
   appended to the transport array as `{ v: 2, iv, ct }`. The format
   version and the snapshot flag are bound into the GCM tag as
   additional authenticated data.
3. **Inbound:** each envelope that appears in the transport array (from
   a peer or from the persistence server) is decrypted and applied to
   the plaintext doc with origin `e2e-remote`. The outbound listener
   ignores that origin, so received edits are never encrypted again
   (no update loop). If decryption fails, the envelope is dropped and
   the user sees an error. Unauthenticated bytes are never applied.
4. **Late joiners:** a peer that joins later receives the whole
   transport array through the normal Yjs sync, decrypts every envelope
   and rebuilds the document. Yjs buffers updates that arrive before
   their dependencies, so envelopes can be decrypted in any order.
5. **Compaction:** when the array grows past 500 envelopes, the peer
   that just wrote one encrypts a full-state snapshot (`s: 1`) and
   deletes only the envelopes it has already applied. A peer that has
   ever failed to decrypt something never compacts, so it can't throw
   away history it couldn't read.

## Who can read what

| Party | Document text & comments | Room name | Envelope count, sizes, timing | Presence: names, colours, cursor anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peer with the password | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Peer without the password | **No** | Yes | Only through a persistence server it can reach | **No** — it can't complete the WebRTC handshake |
| Signaling server | **No** | Yes | Traffic shape only (its messages are encrypted with the password) | **No** |
| persistent collab server (Hocuspocus) | **No** (it stores only ciphertext) | Yes | Yes | **No** — Lumen publishes no presence to it |
| Network eavesdropper | No (WebRTC is DTLS-encrypted anyway) | Depends on the signaling transport | Traffic shape | No |

### Persistent rooms store only ciphertext

With [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) the persistent server
syncs the **transport** doc. Its database holds the envelope array and
never a key, so a leaked server backup reveals no document content. A
peer that joins later still needs the password to read the history.

## Limits: what this does *not* protect

- **Awareness / presence reaches every peer that holds the password.**
  The room password is also given to y-webrtc, which encrypts all
  signaling and BroadcastChannel traffic with a key derived from it, and
  peer connections are DTLS-encrypted — so the signaling server and peers
  *without* the password never see display names, colours or cursors.
  Presence itself is not wrapped in Lumen's envelopes, though: every
  password holder sees it. Cursor positions are Yjs *relative positions*
  (item IDs: client id + clock, no document text). The persistent
  persistent server receives no presence from Lumen.
- **Metadata:** room name, number of peers, number and size of
  envelopes, and when they are written. Size and timing can hint at
  how much is being typed.
- **Integrity of the history as a whole.** Each envelope is
  authenticated, but a malicious relay or persistence server can
  *drop* or *withhold* envelopes, or delete them from the array. That
  makes peers diverge or lose edits, but it can never inject or alter
  content. Replayed envelopes are harmless because Yjs updates are
  idempotent.
- **Anyone with the password.** All peers who know it are trusted
  equally. A peer with the password can also delete envelopes from the
  shared array.
- **Weak passwords.** The key comes only from the password and the room
  name, both of which a server operator knows. An attacker holding the
  ciphertext can run an offline guessing attack, slowed by 200 000
  PBKDF2 iterations per guess. Use a long passphrase.
- **No forward secrecy, no key rotation inside a room.** A password
  that leaks later decrypts all stored history. To rotate, create a
  new room with a new password (see below).
- **Local storage.** Version-history snapshots and saved files on each
  peer are plaintext on that device. Use a Vault password
  (`⌘K → Encrypt document`) for at-rest encryption.

## Rotating

The key is tied to the room, so the clean way to rotate is to move to
a new room with a new password:

```js
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "new-stronger-passphrase");
```

Then leave and start a fresh room, seeding it from your current
document. If you change the password while staying in the same room,
peers on the old password get "Can't decrypt" errors, and the old
history stays encrypted under the old key on any persistence server.

## Trade-offs

- A misplaced password locks everyone out. Treat it like any shared
  secret and share it through a side channel (Signal, 1Password, etc.).
- The PBKDF2 derivation runs once per password and room. That is about
  100 ms on modern devices, but noticeable on old phones.
- Each edit batch adds about 40 bytes of overhead (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing). Long sessions grow the array until compaction
  kicks in at 500 envelopes.

pages.title: Live canvas
pages.description: Draw on one canvas together during a collab session — edits and pointers appear as they happen, over the same encrypted room as the note.
pages.md:
When you share a note in a live session, the canvas you open is shared too.
Everyone in the room who opens the same canvas (same name) sees the others'
shapes, text and arrows change as they draw, and their pointers with their
names.

## How it works

- The canvas travels in the session's document, next to the note. In a room
  with a password it is end-to-end encrypted like the note. On the public
  server, the room only lets in people who hold the share link's password
  ([persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)). Nothing about the drawing
  reaches a server in the clear.
- Two people can change the same shape at the same moment. Lumen uses
  Excalidraw's own rule: every change of a shape has a version number, and
  the later one wins. On a tie, every copy picks the same one. All copies end
  on the same drawing, in whatever order the changes arrive.
- What you are dragging, resizing or typing in stays as you have it until
  you let go.
- A change made by someone else doesn't go into your undo history: ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z
  undoes only your own changes.
- A deleted shape is deleted for everyone.

Each person's copy is still saved to their own vault
(`canvases/<name>.excalidraw`). JSON Canvas export and the note cards work as
on a canvas of your own.

## Limits

- Images added to a live canvas are not sent to the others yet. They see the
  frame where the image is.
- The target is 5,000 shapes at 60 frames per second, and a change seen by
  the others within 150 ms (95th percentile). The nightly run measures the
  frame rate on a real computer. The tests measure the delay over a simulated
  relay.

pages.title: Persistent rooms
pages.description: Keep a collaboration room alive when every peer has left, with a small y-websocket server you run yourself.
pages.md:
A plain [WebRTC room](/collab/webrtc/) lives only in the browsers that are
in it: when the last person leaves, the room is gone (whoever saved the
note keeps their copy). A **persistent server** keeps each room's
document, so anyone can join later and find the latest version, even when
nobody else is online.

## Run the server

`sync-server/persistent-server.js` is a small
[y-websocket](https://github.com/yjs/y-websocket) server that stores every
room on disk with LevelDB.

```bash
cd sync-server
npm install @y/websocket-server y-leveldb
PORT=4444 node persistent-server.js        # ws://localhost:4444
```

- **Storage:** `YJS_STORAGE_DIR` (default `./.yjs-persistence`). On Fly.io,
  Render or Railway, point it at a mounted volume. The Docker compose
  bundle uses `/data/yjs`.
- **Access token:** start it with `COLLAB_TOKEN=<a long random string>`
  and it accepts only clients that send the same token. Without one,
  anyone who knows a room name can read the room's (encrypted) updates
  and add their own.
- **Health:** `GET /healthz` answers `200 {"ok":true}`.
- Put it behind TLS (`wss://`) before you expose it.

`DEPLOY.md` has the Fly.io steps.

## Point Lumen at it

Set it when you build Lumen:

```bash
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_URL=wss://collab.example.com
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN=<the same COLLAB_TOKEN>   # if the server has one
```

Lumen then connects to the server alongside the peer-to-peer mesh. Where
billing is configured, persistent rooms need a Pro or Team plan; a
self-hosted build without billing has them on.

## What the server can read

Nothing, in a room with a password. The server stores only the
AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes, never the text. Rooms created today
have 128-bit random names and are end-to-end encrypted, so the token is
a second gate, not the only one. What the server does see: room names,
and the size and timing of updates. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/#persistent-rooms-store-only-ciphertext).

pages.title: The public server
pages.description: A free live-share server for everyone that stores only encrypted rooms, deletes idle rooms after 90 days and keeps no IP addresses in its logs.
pages.md:
Live sharing works without any server: browsers connect to each other
directly over [WebRTC](/collab/webrtc/). A server adds two things. People on
different networks find each other (signaling), and a room stays available
when nobody else is online ([persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)).

Lumen's public server does both, free, and **never sees what you write**.

## What the server can and can't see

| | The server |
|---|---|
| The text of your note | **Never.** It accepts only rooms with a password ([end-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/)). Every change is checked before it is applied. A change that is not an encrypted envelope closes the connection, and nothing of it is stored. |
| The room's encrypted document | Stored, so a room survives everyone leaving. It is ciphertext. Without the room password nobody can read it, the server included. |
| Who may join a room | Only someone with the room password. The app proves it holds the password with a value derived from it, which is not the encryption key. The server keeps only a hash of that value. The room's name on the server carries a commitment to that hash, so the room accepts only the value that matches it, even from the first person to connect. Knowing a room's name is not enough to join it, write to it, keep it or lock its owners out. A new room also costs the app a few seconds of work. |
| How many new rooms | Limited per day: 2,000 on the whole server, 20 per address (an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 /64) and 80 per IPv6 /48. What is stored is limited too: 20,000 rooms, 4 GB in all, and 50 rooms and 20 MB per address and per IPv6 /48. When the server is full, a new room takes the place of stored rooms that nobody else joined again in the last 14 days and nobody is connected to: the smallest one that frees one room's share of the space, or else a few smaller ones that free it together. Your own return doesn't count (from the same address, or from the same IPv6 /48); a return from another address does. The rooms of an address or /48 that has grown past its 20 MB go first, even if someone came back to them. What you write in someone else's room counts toward your 20 MB, not theirs. A request that can't get a room removes none (it still counts toward that address's 20 a day). Addresses are counted under a keyed hash that changes every day, never stored as such; a stored room keeps only a 20-bit hash of the address that made it, which about 4,000 IPv4 addresses share. pages.title: Encrypted share link
pages.description: Share a read-only copy of one note as a link that carries the note itself, encrypted. No server, no account.
pages.md:
**Share as encrypted link** (command palette) turns the open note into a link. The note
is compressed and encrypted on your device and travels **inside the link**. Whoever opens
the link sees a read-only copy, decrypted in their own browser. Nothing is uploaded, and
neither of you needs an account.

## Why no server sees it

The link looks like this:

```text
https://lumen-md.vercel.app/#view=<encrypted note>&key=<key>
```

Everything after `#` is the *fragment*. Browsers never send it to a server: it is not
part of the request, and it is not in the `Referer` header. So the server that serves
Lumen gets a plain request for its home page, with no byte of the note or of the key.
The tests check this: `e2e/share-link.spec.ts` records every request the viewer makes,
its headers and its body included.

- **Encryption:** AES-GCM with a 256-bit key, made at random for each link (WebCrypto).
  If one character of the link changes, or the key is wrong, the note does not open. It
  never shows altered text.
- **Compression:** `deflate-raw` (CompressionStream) runs before encryption, so a typical
  note of 20 KB makes a link of about 7,000 to 11,000 characters.
- **Read-only:** the viewer shows the note. It does not save the note into the
  recipient's notes, but they can copy the Markdown or download it as `.md`.

## Options

- **Expires:** never, or after 1, 7 or 30 days. The date is inside the encrypted note,
  and the viewer refuses the note after it. This is a promise of the viewer, not of the
  cryptography: the link still holds the note, so someone who kept it could decode it by
  hand.
- **Send the key separately:** you get the link without its key, and the key on its
  own. Send them by two different routes (for example, an email and a message). Someone
  who opens the link without the key is asked to paste it.

## Large notes

A link holds at most 32,768 characters of encrypted data, so that it stays usable in
browsers and in messaging apps. For a larger note, the dialog offers an **encrypted
file** (`.lumenshare`) and a short link that holds only its key. The recipient opens the
link and picks the file. The file is decrypted on their device too.

Opening a link or a file inflates the note at most 100 times its compressed size,
so a crafted link can't freeze the viewer. Every note Lumen shares fits that bound.

## Which address the link opens

A link opens the viewer on a web address the recipient can reach. A link made in the
desktop or mobile app, or on `localhost`, names the public app,
`https://lumen-md.vercel.app` (a build can name another one with `VITE_SHARE_ORIGIN`).
A Lumen served over https from a public host keeps its own address.

## Who can read it

Anyone who has the whole link (or the file and its key link), and nobody else. Treat
the link like the note itself: don't post it where others can read it.

pages.title: Sharing, roles and comment threads
pages.description: Share a note to view, comment or edit with a link that expires; revoke it; comment threads with mentions.
pages.md:
With a [persistent collab server](/collab/webrtc/), a note in a
collaboration session can be shared with a **link that gives one role and
expires**. The server holds everyone to their role, also in end-to-end
encrypted rooms.

## Share a note

1. Start a collaboration session (⌘K → *Start collaboration*).
2. ⌘K → **Share this note…**.
3. Choose the access and the expiry, optionally who it is for, and press
   **Create link**. The link is copied.

| Access | Can |
|---|---|
| **Can view** | read the note and its comments, see who is there |
| **Can comment** | also write, answer and resolve comments |
| **Can edit** | also change the note |

Links expire after 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week or 30 days. The link contains the
room's key (so the note can be decrypted) and the link's id (what the server
checks). Send it only to the person it is for.

## Revoke a link

⌘K → **Share this note…** lists the note's links with their state. Press
**Revoke**: the server stops letting that link in at once and drops anyone
still connected with it **within a few seconds** (the server checks every
second). Their copy of the room key opens nothing without the server.

## Shared with me

⌘K → **Shared with me** lists the links you opened on this device, with
their access and whether they are still active, expired or revoked.

## Comment threads

Select text and add a comment (⌘K → *Add comment*). A comment stays on
its words while others edit around it, in Hebrew too. Write `@name` to
mention someone (also after a Hebrew prefix, as in `ו-@דנה`), answer in
the thread, and resolve it when done.

The threads are kept in the room and, for the note's owner and editors, in
a file next to the note: `plan.md` → `plan.comments.json`. It travels with
the vault (git, sync, export). When the note is shared again, its threads
come back and are placed on their quoted text.

## How it is enforced

- The first time you share a note, your device **claims the room** with an
  owner secret kept in its encrypted secret store; the server keeps only its
  hash. After that, only the owner gets editor access without a link.
- A room with share links is synced **through the server only**, not over
  the peer-to-peer WebRTC mesh, which could not hold anyone to a role.
- Each room has two documents on the server: the note and its comments.
  "Can view" may write neither, "Can comment" only the comments, "Can edit"
  both. A change sent by someone without the right is dropped, along with
  their connection.
- In the app, a view or comment link opens the note read-only and hides
  the comment controls a viewer can't use.
- Collab cursors and name labels follow the line's direction, so they sit
  on the right side of the caret in Hebrew and Arabic text, and a name in
  one script never reorders text in another.

## For server operators

`sync-server/collab-server.mjs` stores rooms' owners and share links in
its SQLite database (no document content). `COLLAB_REVOKE_CHECK_MS`
(default 1000) sets how often live connections of revoked or expired links
are dropped.

pages.title: Suggestions and named versions
pages.description: Suggest edits that change nothing until someone accepts them, accept or reject one person's suggestions at a time, see who wrote what (the AI included), and name versions to compare word by word.
pages.md:
## Suggesting, alone or together

Turn on **suggesting mode** (track changes) from the command palette. From
then on, what you type and delete is written as a suggestion, and the text
itself doesn't change until someone accepts it:

```md
The report is {++almost ++}{>>@Dana<<}done{--, finally--}{>>@Avi<<}.
```

This works in the source editor and in WYSIWYG, alone and in a shared note.
In a shared note, everyone sees each suggestion as it is made.

## Who suggested what

- Each author's suggestions are underlined in their own colour, and hovering
  shows the name.
- Suggestions the AI made carry the author **AI** and are marked "AI".
- The command palette lists everyone who has a suggestion in the note:
  **Accept all from Dana (3)** and **Reject all from Dana (3)**, and the same
  for each other author, the AI included. These resolve only that person's
  suggestions; everyone else's stay as they are.

## Named versions

In a shared note, open **Named versions…** from the command palette.

- Give the current text a name, such as "Before submission". The version is
  saved inside the shared note, so everyone in it sees the same list. Only
  editors can save a version.
- Pick any two versions, or a version and the current text, to compare them.
  The comparison is word by word: additions are green, removals are red, and
  you see how many words were added and removed.
- The comparison is built for Hebrew. A word keeps its one-letter prefixes
  (ו, ה, ב, ל, מ, ש, כ), its niqqud, and a geresh or gershayim inside it
  (צה״ל), so "הבית" changed to "ובית" shows as one changed word, not one
  changed letter.

## Tested

- Twenty Hebrew comparison cases, covering prefixes, niqqud, gershayim,
  numbers, punctuation and mixed Hebrew and English, are checked on every
  run.
- By-author accept and reject are tested to change only that author's
  suggestions.
- A two-browser test runs through the collaboration server. A participant
  suggests and the owner's text doesn't change. The owner accepts and the
  change lands. A version named by the owner then shows up for the
  participant, with the word-level comparison.

pages.title: Real-time WebRTC collaboration
pages.description: Multi-cursor editing over a peer-to-peer mesh — no server account, no central log of your doc.
pages.md:
Lumen ships a real-time collab mode powered by [Yjs](https://yjs.dev)
over WebRTC. Open a doc, share the room link, and every keystroke
syncs to every peer in <30 ms.

## Start a session

`⌘K → Start collaboration`. A toast confirms the room name + copies
the share link to your clipboard:

```
https://lumen.app/#room=lumen-bright-river-77
```

Anyone with the link enters the same Y.Doc. Their cursor + selection
appears in your editor, coloured by their auto-assigned chip.

## Awareness UI

Each peer publishes:

- **Display name** — random adjective+noun combo, e.g. "Marble".
- **Colour** — auto-picked HSL hue.
- **Cursor + selection** — re-published on every selection change.

The editor renders peer cursors with a small floating name tag above
the caret. A peer's selection highlights with a translucent version of
their colour. The list of active peers shows in the status bar.

## End-to-end encryption

Without a password, the room is **not** end-to-end encrypted. Peers sync
the plaintext Yjs document, so any signaling server that relays
messages, the persistent collab server and anyone with the room link can
read it.

Set `localStorage["lumen.collab.password"]` (or append `&password=…` to
the share link) to change that. The editor's document then stays
local, and only AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes (key = PBKDF2 of the
password, salted with the room name) go to the mesh and to any
persistence server. Peers without the password receive only ciphertext
and see a "Can't decrypt this room" error.

The password also encrypts y-webrtc's signaling, so a peer without it
can't connect at all and relays never see presence (names, colours,
cursor positions) — only peers holding the password do. Metadata such
as the room name and the volume and timing of edits is still visible.
A wrong password therefore looks like an empty room: Lumen asks before
sharing your document into it rather than forking the room silently. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/) for the full threat model.

## Rooms evaporate when the last peer leaves

WebRTC is peer-to-peer — there's no server holding the doc. The doc
state lives in each peer's Y.Doc, replicated over the mesh. Once
everyone leaves, the state is only in the OPFS workspace of whoever
saved it. To get persistent rooms (the Notion / Google Docs feel),
enable [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/).

## Comments / annotations

Inline comments anchor to text ranges via Yjs `RelativePosition`, so a
comment on "neural networks" stays attached to those words even when
collaborators insert paragraphs above. Open the comments panel from
`⌘K → View comments panel`.

## Performance budget

- Room cap: 20 simultaneous peers (raise via the WebRTC provider's
  `maxConns`).
- Per-update overhead in password rooms: ≈ 40 bytes (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing) per edit batch; edits made in the same tick share
  one envelope.
- Initial join: full Y.Doc snapshot synced via the signaling channel
  (≈ 1 KB per 1k characters of doc).

For documents larger than ~50k characters or sessions with >20 peers,
move to [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) which uses
the persistent collab server (Hocuspocus + SQLite, `sync-server/collab-server.mjs`).

pages.description: The bundle budgets and the performance gate's FCP and LCP limits are lowered after every train to what the train measured plus 2 %, and never raised. Exceptions carry an expiry date and fail once it has passed.
pages.md:
Lumen's size and speed limits only move one way: down (plan W6.26).
A budget that stays put after a saving invites the next growth.

## Where the limits live

| File | What it limits | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| `scripts/bundle-budgets.json` | Each chunk class (KB gzipped, per file) and the startup total | `npm run budget` |
| `perf-gate.config.json` | FCP and LCP of each profile, and the other metrics | `npm run perf:gate` |
| `lighthouserc.json` | Lighthouse scores and metrics | `npm run lighthouse` |

The first rule in `bundle-budgets.json` whose pattern matches a file
name sets that file's budget, so narrower patterns come first.

## After each train: the ratchet

The train's Vercel build runs the budget gate, which writes the
receipt `reports/bundle-sizes.json` and prints it as one
`bundle-sizes: {…}` line in the build log. Feed either one to the ratchet:

```bash
npm run budget:ratchet -- --sizes reports/bundle-sizes.json --train train-3 --sha <head>
npm run budget:ratchet -- --sizes-log vercel-build.log --perf perf-gate.json --first-party startup.log --write
```

- Each budget becomes the biggest measured file of its class plus 2 %
  (at least 1 KB), rounded up to a whole KB, but only when that is
  lower than the budget today. The startup total works the same way.
- With `--perf` (the JSON of `npm run perf:gate -- --json`), the FCP
  and LCP limits (`error` and `warn`) become the median run plus 2 %
  (at least 50 ms), when that is lower. Targets don't change.
- `--first-party` takes the log of the offline startup measure
  (`startup first-party: … KB gz`) and records it in the history,
  since the Vite build can't tell our own code from package code.
- Without `--write` it only prints what would go down. With `--write`
  it updates the files and appends a line to `history` in
  `bundle-budgets.json`. Commit that as its own commit.

## Exceptions expire

A rule with `expires` (YYYY-MM-DD) is an exception, and it must also
name the `task` that removes it. Today there is one: the Excalidraw
core module at 740 KB, until 2027-01-15, removed by W1.36. From the day
after its date, `npm run budget` fails until the rule is lowered or
decided again with a new date, and pr:check fails a later date.
To check a build on another day, set `LUMEN_TODAY=YYYY-MM-DD`.

## No raise gets in

- `npm run pr:check` fails a diff that loosens any of the three files.
  It compares the budget each chunk name gets before and after, so a
  raised number, a new rule wider than the one its files fell under, a
  removed rule whose files fall to a bigger one and a reordering all
  count. So do a later or dropped expiry date, a wider margin, a
  performance limit raised, removed or turned from `error` into `warn`,
  fewer runs, and a lower Lighthouse level or score. A budget number
  written into `scripts/bundle-budget.mjs` itself fails too.
- `npm run budget:history` checks every commit of the three files since
  the ratchet began and names any commit that raised a limit. Pass
  `-- --since all` to see the whole history, including the decisions
  made before the ratchet.

When a budget fails, split the chunk or load it lazily. The budget
doesn't move up.

pages.title: Checks on every branch (Vercel)
pages.description: Lumen's gates run in the Vercel build of every branch, without GitHub Actions — what runs, what a red status means, and where the old CI checks went.
pages.md:
`main` and the integration trains (`verify/…`) get a Vercel build when
pushed, and Vercel reports it on the commit as the **Vercel** status; a pull
request's own branch is verified through the train (see
[Builds that are skipped](#builds-that-are-skipped)). That build is Lumen's gate: the build
command is `node scripts/vercel-build.mjs` (in `deploy/vercel.base.json`),
and a preview build runs every check. A pull request with a failing test or
a broken gate gets a red **Vercel** status; a clean one gets a green one.
No GitHub Actions minutes are used.

| Build | What runs, in order |
|---|---|
| Preview (the `verify/…` trains) | build, bundle budget, the secret scan of `dist/`, vitest, e2e (smoke on chromium and firefox), `i18n:check`, hygiene, `docs:sync`, `docs:complete` (every page in both languages, and each Hebrew page with its English page's sections, help anchors and at least 60% of its words), the licence gate, the mutation floor (`mutation:check`) |
| Production (`main`) | build, bundle budget — as before |

The gates stop at the first failure. The build log ends with the gate that
failed and the ones that passed before it, with their times:

```text
✗ vercel-build: the vitest gate failed (212.4 s, exit 1). Passed before it: build 95.1 s, budget 1.2 s.
```

## Builds that are skipped

Vercel builds one deployment at a time, so every queued build delays the
ones behind it. `scripts/vercel-ignore.sh` (the config's `ignoreCommand`)
skips a build before it starts when:

- its branch is neither `main` (production) nor an integration train
  (`verify/…`): a pull request's branch is verified through the train
  (`verify/train-2`), so it does not build on its own. Setting the Vercel
  project variable `LUMEN_BUILD_ALL=1` builds every branch again;
- its commit is no longer the head of its branch: a newer push is queued
  and will be built instead. When the branch head cannot be read (no
  network, a deleted branch), the next rule decides;
- the commit changes nothing the web build reads (Markdown outside `src/`
  and `public/`, the docs site, the other deployables).

A skipped build shows as **Canceled** in Vercel, not as a pass: the
branch's status comes from its newest commit.

## Running the same checks locally

```bash
node scripts/vercel-build.mjs              # the preview set
node scripts/vercel-build.mjs --production # build and budget only
node scripts/vercel-build.mjs --dry-run    # print the gates, run nothing
```

Outside Vercel (no `VERCEL_ENV`) the script runs the preview set, so a
local run is what the branch's build will do. Each gate is also an npm
script of its own: `npm run build`, `npm run budget`, `npm test`,
`npm run e2e:gate` (after `VITE_E2E=1 npm run build`: specs reach the app's modules through `window.__lumenTest`, which only such a build has), `npm run i18n:check`, `npm run hygiene`, `npm run docs:sync`, `npm run docs:complete`,
`npm run licenses`, `npm run secrets:dist` (see
[Secret scan of the build](/security/secret-scan/)).

## What does not run in the build

Checks that need browsers, devices or signing keys can't run in a Vercel
build. They run in a Vercel Sandbox (W1.1) or on a developer machine:

| Plan task | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| 8.3 Lighthouse gate | an LHCI job on every PR | `npm run lighthouse` (median of 5 runs, the thresholds in `lighthouserc.json`) in the Sandbox, against the preview's build; not a build step, since it needs Chromium |
| 0.19 PR gate (Danger.js, size-limit) | a Danger comment and size-limit on every PR | the size part is the **bundle budget** gate (every main chunk has a budget, `scripts/bundle-budget.mjs`); an unlisted network call fails **vitest** (`src/__tests__/cloudRoutes.test.ts` audits every cloud route); the licence diff is the **licence gate**. The PR comment itself has no replacement yet |
| 13.3 Android and iOS builds | mobile builds in CI | `npm run android:sync` / `npm run ios:sync` on a machine with the SDKs (iOS needs macOS); the web part they ship is what the preview build checks |
| 13.4 Release pipeline | a release workflow | a local release script, signed artifacts and rollback on a developer machine; the web app's release is the production build |
| Playwright e2e | e2e jobs on every PR | the **e2e** gate runs `e2e/smoke.spec.ts` on chromium and firefox in the build (`scripts/e2e-gate.mjs`); the whole suite runs with `npx playwright test` on a developer machine or in the Sandbox (W1.1), since on the build machine the chromium project alone takes about 30 minutes. WebKit cannot run in the build: Playwright's WebKit needs glibc 2.38 and the build image (Amazon Linux 2023) has 2.34. Safari is covered on a Mac (W4.22) |

## When a gate is red

Open the Vercel deployment from the commit's status and read the end of
the build log: the failing gate is named there. Fix it on the branch and
push again; Vercel builds the new commit. A failing gate is never skipped
or loosened to get a green status.

pages.title: Design system
pages.description: Lumen's tokens for colour, space, radius, type, elevation and motion, the rules the code is held to, and the shared components.
pages.md:
Every surface of Lumen draws from one set of tokens. They are CSS custom
properties in `src/index.css`, so dark mode, the theme presets (Settings →
Theme) and *reduce motion* change them in one place. Inline styles use them
through `src/ui/tokens.ts`.

## Tokens

| Group | Tokens | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Surfaces and text | `--bg`, `--bg-subtle`, `--bg-muted`, `--bg-inset`, `--fg`, `--fg-subtle`, `--fg-muted`, `--border`, `--border-strong`, `--accent`, `--accent-fg` | HSL triplets: `hsl(var(--bg))`, `hsl(var(--accent) / 0.15)` |
| Status | `--danger`, `--success`, `--warning`, `--info` | errors and destructive actions, confirmations, cautions, information; tuned for light and dark |
| Gradients | `--gradient-brand`, `--gradient-ai`, `--gradient-success` | the logo, the AI button, progress — decoration only |
| Behind a modal | `--overlay` | every dialog backdrop |
| Elevation | `--shadow-sm`, `--shadow-md`, `--shadow-lg`, `--shadow-xl`, `--shadow-accent` | badges, popovers, menus, dialogs; the accent glow |
| Space | `--space-1` … `--space-8` (4 px steps) | padding and gaps |
| Radius | `--radius-sm` 4, `--radius-md` 6, `--radius-lg` 10, `--radius-full` | |
| Type | `--text-xs` 11 … `--text-xl` 18 px | |
| Motion | `--duration-fast` 100 ms, `--duration-base` 250 ms, `--duration-slow` 350 ms; `--ease-out`, `--ease-in-out` | menus and hovers; dialogs and toasts; panels |

In TypeScript: `color.danger`, `color.tint("danger", 0.1)`, `shadow.lg`,
`transition(["opacity"], "base")`, `enter("cmdSlideIn")`. A `<canvas>`
cannot read `var()`: use `resolvedColor("fg", 0.15)` when drawing.

## Rules

1. **No hard-coded colour in the interface** — no hex, `rgb()` or `hsl()`
   with numbers in `src/ui`, nor in the other folders that draw dialogs,
   panels and blocks (`COLOR_SCOPE` in `scripts/check-design.mjs`: sign-in,
   sync, backup, tasks, views, plugins, and more). Colours a person picks
   for their content (the note colours of the canvas) are content, and so
   is a QR code, which stays black on white for the camera; both are marked
   `design-allow`.
2. **Only `transform` and `opacity` move**, with the three durations.
   Nothing animates width, height, top/left or margins: a progress bar
   scales (`transform: scaleX()`), a menu slides (`translateY`), a hover
   changes colour instantly.
3. **Reduce motion is respected everywhere**: with the system setting on,
   the duration tokens become 0 and a global rule cuts every remaining
   animation.
4. **Logical sides**: `marginInlineStart`, `insetInlineEnd`, `textAlign:
   "start"` — a surface mirrors in Hebrew by itself. Viewport coordinates
   from `getBoundingClientRect()` stay physical.
5. **A modal backdrop is `var(--overlay)`; a shadow is a step of the scale.**

`npm run design:check` runs both gates: `scripts/check-design.mjs` (rules
1 on the interface folders, rule 2 on all of `src/ui`, and no layout
animation anywhere in `src`) and `scripts/design-audit.mjs`, which runs the
checklist (rules 1, 2, 4, 5) on the 43 surfaces listed in
`scripts/design-surfaces.json`. A bare name there is `src/ui/<name>.tsx`; a
name with a folder, such as `sync/cloud/ConflictDialog`, is a surface outside
`src/ui`. A real exception is
marked `design-allow: <reason>` in the code.

## Shared components

| Component | Where | For |
|---|---|---|
| Dialogs | `uiAlert`, `uiConfirm`, `uiPrompt`, `uiSelect` (`src/ui/PromptDialog.tsx`) | every question and confirmation; never `window.confirm` |
| Modal frame | `.cmd-palette-backdrop` + `.cmd-palette` (`src/ui/CommandPalette.css`) | panels such as the trash, the AI doctor, settings |
| Toasts | `showAiToast()` (`src/ui/AiToast.tsx`), `toast.*` (`src/store/useToastStore.ts`) | short messages; `action` for an Undo |
| Icon button | `.icon-btn` (`src/index.css`) | toolbar and panel buttons |
| Command palette | `src/ui/CommandPalette.tsx` | every action has a command |

pages.title: Independent review
pages.description: Every change to a sensitive path needs a review receipt for its head commit from a reviewer that did not write it, with attack tests, before it is merged — integration trains included.
pages.md:
A change to a sensitive path — the paths `.github/CODEOWNERS` lists:
cryptography, vault writes, the privacy ledger, CSP and security policy,
sanitisers, native permissions and updates — is reviewed by someone who did
not write it before it is merged. This holds for the fixes an integration
train (`verify/*`) makes while it resolves conflicts in that code: the
train's own PR needs a review too. A person still adds the `human-reviewed`
label as well (see [Second maintainer](/contributing/second-maintainer/));
this page is the reviewer's part.

## The rule

`npm run pr:check` has the check **Independent review of sensitive paths**.
When a sensitive file changed it needs a **review receipt** that:

1. names the PR's head commit (all 40 characters). A push after the review
   makes the receipt stale, and a new review is needed;
2. has a reviewer that is not the author (another lane or agent, or a
   person), with `"access": "read-only"`: the reviewer could not push to the
   branch;
3. covers every sensitive file in the diff (`files`: paths or CODEOWNERS
   patterns);
4. lists at least one attack test the reviewer wrote or ran, with its result;
5. has no finding of severity `critical` or `high` still `open`, and the
   verdict `approve`.

With `--pr <n>` the receipts are read from the PR's comments, and the check
fails without one that counts. With `--review <file>` (repeatable) a
receipt file is checked against this checkout's `HEAD`, offline. With
neither, the check only warns.

## The receipt

Post it as a PR comment with a fenced block whose language is
`lumen-review`, or keep it as a JSON file:

````md
```lumen-review
{
  "format": "lumen-review",
  "version": 1,
  "pr": 495,
  "head": "<40-character sha of the reviewed head>",
  "author": "train-2",
  "reviewer": "S",
  "access": "read-only",
  "date": "2026-11-12T18:00:00Z",
  "files": ["/src/sync/e2ee/lan/"],
  "attackTests": [
    { "path": "src/__tests__/lanPreAuthAttack.test.ts", "result": "6/6 pass", "failsWithoutFix": 3 }
  ],
  "findings": [
    { "id": "E56-1", "severity": "medium", "status": "fixed", "summary": "…", "fix": "<sha or patch>" }
  ],
  "verdict": "approve"
}
```
````

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `head` | The commit reviewed. Must be the PR's head when the check runs |
| `author`, `reviewer` | Who wrote the change and who reviewed it. Must differ |
| `access` | Always `read-only` |
| `files` | What was reviewed: every sensitive file of the diff must be covered |
| `attackTests` | `path`, `result`, and optionally `failsWithoutFix`: how many of them fail without the fix |
| `findings` | `id`, `severity` (`critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `info`), `status` (`open`, `fixed`, `accepted`), `summary`, `fix` |
| `verdict` | `approve` or `changes-requested` |

## How a reviewer works

- Check out the head read-only (a detached worktree, or `git show`); never
  push to the branch under review.
- Write the threat model down: who the attacker is, what they can already
  do, and what the change adds.
- Write attack tests for it and run them; when you find a problem, show
  that the test fails without your fix.
- Put the fix in a patch or a separate PR for the author; then post the
  receipt for the head you reviewed.

sections.text: npm run pr:check has the check Independent review of sensitive paths . When a sensitive file changed it needs a review receipt that: 1. names the PR's head commit (all 40 characters). A push after the review makes the receipt stale, and a new review is needed; 2. has a reviewer that is not the author (another lane or agent, or a person), with "access": "read-only": the reviewer could not push to the branch; 3. covers every sensitive file in the diff (files: paths or CODEOWNERS patterns); 4. lists at least one attack test the reviewer wrote or ran, with its result; 5. has no finding of severity critical or high still open, and the verdict approve. With --pr the receipts are read from the PR's comments, and the check fails without one that counts. With --review (repeatable) a receipt file is checked against this checkout's HEAD, offline. With neither, the check only warns.

sections.heading: The receipt

Must be the PR's head when the check runs author, reviewer Who wrote the change and who reviewed it. Must differ access Always read-only files What was reviewed: every sensitive file of the diff must be covered attackTests path, result, and optionally failsWithoutFix: how many of them fail without the fix findings id, severity (critical, high, medium, low, info), status (open, fixed, accepted), summary, fix verdict approve or changes-requested

Write attack tests for it and run them; when you find a problem, show that the test fails without your fix. Put the fix in a patch or a separate PR for the author; then post the receipt for the head you reviewed.

pages.title: Compiling the native code offline
pages.description: How Lumen's Rust, Java and Swift code is compiled without crates.io, the Android SDK or Xcode — what the check proves, what it cannot, and what still needs a Mac.
pages.md:
Lumen has native code next to the web app: the Tauri desktop shell in
`src-tauri/` (Rust), the Android plugins and widget (Java), and the iOS
extensions (Swift). A full build needs crates.io, the WebKitGTK headers, the
Android SDK with Google's Maven repository, or Xcode. When none of those are
reachable (an offline sandbox, a plane, a blocked network), run:

```sh
bash tools/native-check/run.sh
```

It needs only `rustc` and `javac` (JDK 17 or newer), and finishes in about
ten seconds.

## What it checks

| Step | What runs | What a pass proves |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Std-only crates | `rustc --test` on `src-tauri/desktop`, `keychain`, `vault`, `src/whisper_core.rs` | The code compiles and its unit tests pass — for real, no stubs. |
| 2. The Tauri glue | `rustc` on `src-tauri/src/lib.rs` + `main.rs` against `tools/native-check/rust-stubs/`, once with `--cfg desktop` and once with `--cfg mobile` | Every module, import, type, borrow and lifetime checks out against the signatures of tauri 2 and its plugins. |
| 2. Commands | the stub `#[tauri::command]` | Each argument is a command argument (Deserialize, `State`, `AppHandle`, `Window`, `Request`), each return value is an IPC response, every async command's future is `Send`, and an async command that borrows returns a `Result` — the rules the real macro enforces. |
| 2. Cargo.lock | `lockcheck.mjs` | Every dependency in `Cargo.toml` is in `Cargo.lock`: `cargo check --locked` would not refuse it. |
| 3. Android | `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` on `android/app/src/main/java` and `mobile/android` against `java-stubs/`, with an `R` class generated from `res/` | The Java compiles with no warnings; every `@string`, `@xml`, `@layout`, `@drawable`, `@mipmap` and `@style` reference exists. |
| 4. Swift | listed only | Nothing: Swift needs Xcode. |

## What it cannot prove

The stubs hold signatures, not behaviour. They were copied from tauri 2 and
from the plugin sources (tauri-plugin-dialog, -deep-link, -single-instance,
-updater, -fs) at the versions in `Cargo.lock`. A stub can be wrong, and when
the code uses an API the stubs lack, add it there **from the real source**,
never to make an error go away. These still need the real tools:

- `cargo check --locked` / `npm run tauri:build` (needs crates.io, and on
  Linux `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev`, `libgtk-3-dev`, `libayatana-appindicator3-dev`);
- code under `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` or `"windows"` (the keychain, macOS
  `RunEvent::Opened`): the check runs for the Linux target only;
- `./gradlew assembleDebug` in `android/` (Android SDK + Google Maven);
- the Swift files and the widget/intents targets: Xcode on a Mac
  (see [Android and iOS builds](/self-hosting/mobile/)).

## When it fails

Each failure names the file and line, as `rustc` and `javac` print them. A
failure in step 2 that names a tauri item the stubs do not have
(`no method named … found`) means either a real bug or a missing stub: look
the item up in the tauri source for the version in `Cargo.lock` before
changing either side.

pages.title: Nightly runs and receipts
pages.description: npm run nightly runs the flake hunt, the perf checks, the review triage and the weekly health on your own machine, and writes a signed report for each, without GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
Lumen doesn't use GitHub Actions, so the scheduled runs (plan 0.11) and the
measurements that depend on them (0.5: three nights with no flaky test; 0.14:
how many preview-build failures a local `ci:local` run would have caught) run
on the owner's machine. One command does it:

```bash
npm run nightly                  # what is due today
npm run nightly -- --dry-run     # print the plan, run nothing
```

| Kind | When | What runs |
|---|---|---|
| `flake` | every night | `npm run e2e:flake -- --all --times 5` (chromium, firefox, webkit, 5 runs each, no retries) |
| `perf` | every night | build, bundle budget, the `@nightly` perf project, Lighthouse when it is installed |
| `triage` | every night | review triage of the open PRs, the 0.14 count over the first 20 PRs since 12.11.2026, and `live:meta --self-test` (below) |
| `weekly` | Sundays (UTC) | dependency health (audit, outdated, licences), and mutation scores when `test:mutation` is there |
| `sr` | every night, on a Mac with `@guidepup/*` installed | `npx @guidepup/setup --ci`, then the Hebrew journey under VoiceOver ([screen readers, automated](/editor/screen-reader-automation/)). Not counted by 0.11. |

`--only flake,perf` picks kinds. The scheduler passes `--scheduled`, which
marks the reports as scheduled. Plan 0.11 counts only those.

## Reports and receipts

Each kind writes `reports/nightly/<date>-<kind>.json`. The report records:

- the commit, and whether the tree was clean
- the machine: platform, Node and CPU count, no host name
- every command with its exit code and duration
- the sha256 of each command's output, with its last lines
- the kind's numbers: flaky and always-failing tests per browser, perf
  annotations, review totals, audit counts

The report is **sealed**. It carries its sha256 and an Ed25519 signature
made with a key that never leaves the machine
(`~/.config/lumen-md/nightly-ed25519.pem`, mode 0600, created on the first
run; `LUMEN_NIGHTLY_KEY` overrides the path). The public half is committed as
`reports/nightly/PUBLIC_KEY.pem`. Anyone can check a committed report:

```bash
npm run nightly -- --verify reports/nightly/2026-11-13-flake.json
```

If any number in the report changed after the run, both the digest and the
signature fail.

`reports/nightly/status.json` (sealed too) is recomputed after every run
(`npm run nightly -- --status` does only that). It records:

- **0.5**: how many consecutive nights each had every browser 5 times, with
  no flaky and no always-failing test (3 are needed)
- **0.11**: which of the four kinds produced a scheduled report (all 4 are
  needed)
- **0.14**: in the first 20 PRs opened since 12.11.2026, the commits whose
  **Vercel** preview build failed. The preview build runs a subset of
  `ci:local`, so each such failure is one `ci:local` would have caught,
  except `docs:sync`, which `ci:local` doesn't run. `verify/*` integration
  branches aren't counted.

`--commit` commits `reports/nightly/` with a `[skip ci]` message. It never
pushes. A commit that changes only `reports/` doesn't start a Vercel build
(`scripts/vercel-ignore.sh`), so receipts don't use up the deployment quota.

## Scheduling it on a Mac (launchd)

Use a clone that is used only for the nightly, on its own branch, so a run
never mixes with your work:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md ~/lumen-nightly
cd ~/lumen-nightly && git switch -c nightly/receipts && npm ci && npx playwright install
```

Save `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.lumen-md.nightly.plist`:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>dev.lumen-md.nightly</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/bin/zsh</string><string>-lc</string>
    <string>cd ~/lumen-nightly && git pull -q --rebase origin main && npm ci --silent && npm run nightly -- --scheduled --commit</string>
  </array>
  <key>StartCalendarInterval</key><dict><key>Hour</key><integer>2</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>17</integer></dict>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/tmp/lumen-nightly.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/tmp/lumen-nightly.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
```

Then load it with `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.lumen-md.nightly.plist`.
launchd runs a job that was missed while the Mac slept as soon as it wakes.
To publish the receipts, push the branch (`git push origin nightly/receipts`)
or open a PR from it. Linux uses cron instead:

```text
17 2 * * *  cd ~/lumen-nightly && git pull -q --rebase origin main && npm ci --silent && npm run nightly -- --scheduled --commit
```

## Why not Vercel Cron or a cloud scheduled task

- **Vercel Cron** only calls a function of a deployment on a schedule. It
  can't run three browsers five times over the e2e suite, and it would spend
  the shared deployment quota.
- **A Claude Code scheduled task** starts a fresh cloud session. That session
  has no browsers and can't install packages, so it can run only the
  `triage` kind (GitHub's REST API) and read the committed receipts. That is
  useful for a morning summary, not for the measurements themselves.

## Live metadata check (plan W6.2)

`npm run live:meta` fetches the production `index.html`, `robots.txt` and
`sitemap.xml` and fails unless the canonical link, `og:url`, `og:image`,
`twitter:image`, every URL in the JSON-LD, the `Sitemap:` line and every
sitemap `<loc>` point at `lumen-md.vercel.app`, and the domain the project
doesn't own appears nowhere in them. The pattern for that domain is built from
parts in `scripts/lib/liveMeta.mjs`, the same way the PR gate builds it, so
the repository never contains it.

```bash
npm run live:meta                                   # production, after every deploy
npm run live:meta -- --url https://<deployment>.vercel.app
npm run live:meta -- --dir dist                     # a build, before deploying it
npm run live:meta -- --self-test --json live-meta.json
```

`--self-test` first checks a clean copy of the pages. Then it plants a
foreign reference in each place (canonical, `og:image`, `og:url` on another
host, body text, `Sitemap:`, `<loc>`) and fails if the check misses any of
them.

Run it **after every production deploy**: the owner's merge session runs it
right after promoting. Every night the `triage` kind runs it too, so drift
shows up within a day. The command exits 1 on any problem. It fetches with
Node and falls back to `curl`, which follows `HTTPS_PROXY`.

pages.title: The PR check
pages.description: npm run pr:check is the local PR gate that replaces Danger.js and size-limit. It reports bundle size against the base, PR body sections, [skip ci] commits, unregistered network calls, licences and the domain rule.
pages.md:
Lumen runs no GitHub Actions on pull requests. Danger.js and size-limit
need Actions, so one local command replaces them (plan 0.19):

```bash
npm run build
npm run pr:check -- --base origin/main --body pr-body.md --build-base --out pr-check.md
```

The report is Markdown. Paste it into the pull request. The command exits
with 1 when a check fails. Warnings do not fail it.

## The checks

- **Bundle size.** The gzipped size of each chunk class (`npm run budget -- --json`),
  compared with the base, as a table. The bundle budget's own verdict
  decides pass or fail. The base's sizes come from one of:
  - `--base-sizes <file>`;
  - `--build-base`, which builds the merge base in a temporary worktree
    that links this checkout's `node_modules`.
- **Commits.** Every subject from the merge base to `HEAD` contains
  `[skip ci]`.
- **PR body.** The file passed with `--body` has every section, none
  empty:
  - What and why
  - Definition of done (plan 0.7)
  - Local verification
  - Not verified here
  - Owner commands
- **Network.** Every new call that sends a request (`fetch`, `WebSocket`,
  `EventSource`, `sendBeacon`, `importScripts`) goes to a host listed in
  the privacy ledger (`src/ai/privacyLedger.ts`). A call whose URL is
  computed instead needs a `// privacy-ledger: <rule>` comment.
- **Licences.** Every production package added or changed in the
  lockfile has an allowed licence (no copyleft, no non-commercial, not
  missing).
- **Domain.** No added line names the project's domain.
- **Human review (plan W4.28).** A change to a sensitive path — every path
  in `.github/CODEOWNERS`: cryptography, vault writes, the privacy ledger,
  CSP and security policy, native permissions — needs the `human-reviewed`
  label, added by a person after the last commit. With `--pr <n>` the label
  and its time are read from GitHub (`gh api`) and the check fails without
  them; without `--pr` it only warns. Tal runs it with `--pr` before every
  merge. See [Second maintainer](/contributing/second-maintainer/).
- **Sensitive files have an owner (plan W8.6).** Which files are sensitive
  is worked out from the code, not kept by hand
  (`scripts/lib/sensitivePaths.mjs`): shipped code whose path or text shows
  cryptography, an export or publish door, a sanitizer, a frame sandbox,
  CSP or security headers, a network call, redaction, criticMarkup, or the
  Markdown-to-HTML pipeline and its raw-HTML sinks. Each changed file of
  that kind needs a line in `.github/CODEOWNERS`, or an entry in
  `security/codeowners-exceptions.json` with a reason and an expiry date
  (at most 90 days ahead). An expired or undated exception fails. When the
  PR changes CODEOWNERS or the exceptions, the whole tree is checked. The
  report prints the CODEOWNERS lines to add.

The same sensitive paths also need an independent review receipt for the
head commit, from a reviewer that did not write the change, with attack tests
and no critical or high finding open (plan W6.11). See
[Independent review](/contributing/independent-review/).
- **Budgets only go down** (plan W6.26). A diff that raises a bundle
  budget, the startup budget, an exception's expiry date, the ratchet
  margin, a performance-gate FCP/LCP limit or a Lighthouse assertion
  fails. So does a budget number written into `scripts/bundle-budget.mjs`
  itself. See [Budgets that only go down](/contributing/budgets/).

It also warns:
- when source changed and no test did;
- when an AI agent wrote the PR (add the `ai-written` label).

## The branch's base (plan W6.22)

Every PR is based on the current train (the highest-numbered
`verify/train-N` on the remote) or on `main`, not on another PR's branch.
The check:
- warns when the base is something else, and names the
  `scripts/restack.mjs` command that prints how to move it;
- warns when the branch is behind its base (the train head, for a
  stacked PR) and says by how many commits;
- fails when the merge base is more than 7 days old
  (`--max-age-days`), or when there is more than one merge base
  (a criss-cross).

See [Every PR on the train head](/contributing/train-base/).

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--base <ref>` | The branch the PR goes into (default `origin/main`) |
| `--body <file>` | The PR description, to check its sections |
| `--base-sizes <file>`, `--head-sizes <file>` | Sizes already measured |
| `--build-base` | Build the base to measure it |
| `--no-size` | Skip the size check |
| `--pr <n>` | The pull request number: read its labels, label events, reviews and comments (human-review and independent-review rules) |
| `--review <file>` | A review receipt file to check against this checkout's HEAD, offline; repeatable ([Independent review](/contributing/independent-review/)) |
| `--repo <owner/name>` | The repository, when the `origin` remote does not name it |
| `--train <branch>` | The current train, when it isn't the highest `verify/train-N` on the remote |
| `--max-age-days <n>` | The age limit of the merge base (default 7) |
| `--out <file>` | Write the report |

## The whole tree

`npm run codeowners:check` runs the owner check on every file in the
repository and exits with 1 on a gap. `-- --list` also prints every
sensitive file, the rules it matched and the CODEOWNERS line that covers
it. An exception looks like this:

```json
[
  { "path": "src/storage/exportOdt.ts", "reason": "The second maintainer takes it over in W9.1.", "expires": "2027-01-31" }
]
```

pages.title: Before main, WebKit and Safari
pages.description: npm run promote:check refuses to promote main to a commit without a signed WebKit receipt and a signed Safari receipt for that commit. WebKit runs on the verification factory, real Safari on BrowserStack's open-source plan.
pages.md:
The platform that lost notes in the data-safety drill (#470: 376 notes on
Safari's OPFS path) is the one the Vercel build image can't test: WebKit
needs a newer glibc than that image has. So the rule (plan W6.6) is:
**main is never promoted to a commit without a WebKit receipt and a Safari
receipt for that same commit.**

```bash
npm run promote:check                         # the commit you're on
npm run promote:check -- origin/verify/train  # the train you're about to merge
npm run promote:check -- <sha> --pin <key fingerprint>
```

It exits 0 only when both of these hold:

- **WebKit:** a full receipt of the [verification factory](/self-hosting/verification-factory/)
  for that commit, whose `e2e webkit` suite passed (every spec, 4 shards).
  If the data-safety drill ran in that receipt, it passed too.
- **Safari:** passing Safari runs on a real iPhone and on macOS for that
  commit, in a factory receipt or in a separate `safari` receipt.

A receipt counts only when its Ed25519 signature verifies with a host key
from the receipts repository (`keys/<host>.pem`). A receipt for another
commit counts only when that commit has exactly the same tree: a merge into
main that changes nothing else. Pass `--pin` (or set `LUMEN_RECEIPT_KEYS`)
with the fingerprints the factory printed at install time. Without it,
every key in the receipts repository is trusted, and the check says so.

Exit 1 means refused. The output names what is missing or failed. Exit 2
means it couldn't check: an unknown commit, no receipts, or no trusted key.

## WebKit: on the factory

The factory runs every spec in the `webkit` project of `playwright.config.ts`
(Playwright's WebKit, "Desktop Safari" settings) inside Playwright's own
Ubuntu 24.04 image. That image ships WebKit's libraries for amd64 and arm64.
Data safety runs there too: `e2e/data-safety.spec.ts` is part of the full
run, and so is the data-safety drill when the commit has it.

## Safari: BrowserStack's open-source plan

**What the plan gives** (browserstack.com/open-source, checked on 12
November 2026): free, "unlimited testing on desktop and mobile: Live,
Automate and Percy", for **5 users and 5 parallels**, for as long as the
project runs ("lifetime access"). The page names no minutes limit, and it
states no licence, attribution or renewal terms. The application form asks
for a name, an email, a password and the **project URL**.

**What runs:** `npm run safari:run` (the factory runs it for the trains
once credentials are set). It builds the app with the e2e hooks and runs
these specs through BrowserStack's Node SDK, with BrowserStack Local, so
the devices reach the app on the factory itself:

- `e2e/smoke.spec.ts`, `e2e/rtl.spec.ts`, `e2e/first-run.spec.ts`,
  `e2e/locale-switch.spec.ts`, and `e2e/data-safety.spec.ts`
- on **real Safari, iPhone 17 (iOS 26), iPhone 16 (iOS 18), iPhone 15
  (iOS 17)**. The two older versions lack parts of OPFS, and that is the path
  that lost notes.
- on **macOS Sequoia, browser `playwright-webkit`**: BrowserStack runs
  Playwright's WebKit build on a real Mac. That isn't the Safari app.
  Real Safari comes from the iPhones. BrowserStack supports Playwright on
  real iOS Safari since June 2025, with Playwright 1.50.1 or newer.

Each platform becomes its own result: the suite `safari ios 17 (iPhone 15)`,
a commit status, and its device and iOS version in the receipt. That is the
record of which Safari versions were tested.

**Not automated:** the Word (RTL) check and the desktop auto-update in 15.12
still need a person. The Safari part of 15.12 is these specs.

### The owner's step, once BrowserStack approves

1. Apply at **browserstack.com/open-source** with the project URL
   `https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md` (public, MIT).
2. Once approved, copy the **Username** and **Access Key** from the
   Automate dashboard, then from the Mac:

```bash
VM=ubuntu@<the factory's IP>
printf 'BrowserStack username: '; read -r BSU; printf 'Access key: '; read -rs BSK; echo
printf 'BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME=%s\nBROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY=%s\n' "$BSU" "$BSK" | ssh "$VM" 'sudo install -m 600 -o root /dev/stdin /etc/lumen-factory/browserstack.env && sudo systemctl daemon-reload'
unset BSU BSK
```

The factory's systemd unit reads that file if it exists. The credentials
reach the test container as environment variables, never on a command line.
On the Mac fallback, write the same two lines to
`~/lumen-factory/etc/browserstack.env` with `chmod 600`.

Until BrowserStack approves, `promote:check` refuses every promotion of
main. That is the plan's rule, not an accident.

pages.title: Second maintainer
pages.description: Onboarding for Lumen's second maintainer — access, the local checks, how to review a sensitive change and add the human-reviewed label, security reports, and what only the owner holds today.
pages.md:
Lumen has one human maintainer (Tal) and AI agents that open most pull
requests. Code that protects users — cryptography, vault writes, the privacy
ledger, CSP — must not depend on one person or be merged without a person
reading it. This page is everything a second maintainer needs on day one.

## 1. Access (Tal does this, ≈10 minutes)

```sh
# Invite with the Maintain role (merge, labels, advisories; no settings or deletion).
gh api -X PUT repos/talstilkol/lumen-md/collaborators/<login> -f permission=maintain
```

Then Tal adds `@<login>` after `@talstilkol` on each line of
`.github/CODEOWNERS`, in a pull request that he reviews himself (the file is
itself a sensitive path). From then on GitHub requests your review on every
pull request that touches a sensitive path.

## 2. Run everything locally (no GitHub Actions)

The repository runs no GitHub Actions. Every check runs on your machine:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md && cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run typecheck && npx vitest run          # unit and component tests
npm run build && npm run budget              # production build + bundle budget
npx playwright test --project=chromium       # end-to-end
bash tools/native-check/run.sh               # Rust and Java, offline (if present on the branch)
npm run pr:check -- --base origin/<base> --pr <n> --no-size   # the PR gate, before a merge
```

## 3. Reviewing a sensitive change

`npm run pr:check -- --pr <n>` lists the sensitive files a pull request
changes and fails until the `human-reviewed` label is on it, **added after the
last commit**. Agents never add that label: it means "a person read this
diff". Read the diff with the questions for its area:

| Area (paths in `.github/CODEOWNERS`) | Ask |
|---|---|
| Cryptography (`src/sync/e2ee/`, `src/collab/encryption.ts`, `src/storage/vault/encrypted/`, `src/lib/crypto*`, keychain, signing) | Only WebCrypto / platform primitives, no hand-rolled crypto? A fresh random nonce/IV per encryption, never reused with one key? KDF parameters not lowered? Keys never logged, sent, or stored in plain text? Authenticated encryption (GCM) checked before use? |
| Vault writes (`src/storage/vault/`, `src-tauri/vault/`, `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`, the Android SAF plugin) | Every path checked to stay inside the vault (`..`, absolute paths, symlinks)? Writes atomic (temporary file + rename)? A failure leaves the old note intact? |
| Privacy (`src/ai/privacyLedger.ts`, worker ledger, `src/ai/policy.ts`, telemetry) | Does a new host, category or rule let note text, keys or personal data leave the device without a user action? Is the default still local-only? |
| CSP, headers, policy (`src/build/cspEndpoints.ts`, `public/_headers`, `deploy/`, `scripts/headers.mjs`, `security/`) | No new wildcard, `unsafe-*`, or third-party host without a ledger entry? COOP/COEP unchanged unless intended? |
| Sanitisers and plugin sandbox | Untrusted HTML still sanitised? The plugin iframe still without `allow-same-origin`? |
| Native permissions (`src-tauri/capabilities/`, `tauri.conf.json`, `updates.rs`) | No broader `fs:`/`shell:` permission? Updates still signed and from the release host only? |

When it is right: approve the pull request in GitHub (your approval on the
head commit shows in the pr:check report), then add the label:

```sh
gh api -X POST repos/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues/<n>/labels -f "labels[]=human-reviewed"
```

If commits arrive after your review, the check fails again: review the new
commits, remove the label and add it again.

## 4. Security reports

Reports arrive as private GitHub advisories (`SECURITY.md`). Both
maintainers receive them. If Tal has not answered within 48 hours, you own
the report: acknowledge, triage, fix in the advisory's private fork, release,
publish.

## 5. What only the owner holds today

These are single points of failure until they are shared or escrowed; each
is an owner step (plan W4.7):

- the Vercel project and its domain `lumen-md.vercel.app`;
- the desktop updater signing key (minisign) and its password;
- the Apple Developer and Google Play accounts and signing keys;
- the GitHub repository's admin rights.

Recommended: a sealed copy of each key in a password manager shared by both
maintainers (1Password or Bitwarden "emergency access"), and admin rights for
the second maintainer after six months of reviews.

## 6. A second signing key

Each signing key should have a second holder, or a second key that is just as
valid, so that one lost laptop or one absent person stops nothing.

| What is signed | Today | With two maintainers |
|---|---|---|
| Your review and your commits | — | Each maintainer signs commits and tags with their own SSH key: `git config gpg.format ssh`, `git config user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, `git config commit.gpgsign true`, and the key is added on GitHub as a **signing** key. Its fingerprint goes in the table in `SECURITY.md` ("Maintainers and keys"). |
| Registry plugins (Ed25519, [Plugin signing keys](/plugins/signing/)) | Tal's key, if set | **A second key, not a copy.** `VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS` is a JSON map of fingerprint → key, so both maintainers' public keys are trusted side by side. Each signs with their own key (`openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519`), and either can revoke the other's by removing one entry. |
| Desktop updates (minisign, `tauri.conf.json` `plugins.updater.pubkey`) | Tal's key and password | The updater trusts **one** public key, so a second key is not possible. The private key and its password go into the shared emergency vault (section 7). To rotate: ship one release signed with the old key whose config carries the new `pubkey`. After that, releases are signed with the new key. |
| Android and iOS | Tal's accounts | The second maintainer is added to Google Play Console and App Store Connect with a release role. Signing keys go into the emergency vault. |

When the second maintainer joins: generate the keys, put both fingerprints in
`SECURITY.md`, and add `@<login>` to `.github/CODEOWNERS`. Both changes are
sensitive paths, so the other maintainer reviews them.

## 7. Emergency access

If one maintainer disappears, the other must be able to keep users safe: ship
a security fix, revoke a key, keep the site up.

1. **A shared emergency vault.** Use a password manager with delegated
   emergency access, for example Bitwarden's Emergency Access. A premium
   account names a trusted contact (a free account is enough for the
   contact). The contact requests access, and it is granted automatically
   after a wait time the holder chooses, unless the holder rejects it
   ([Bitwarden](https://bitwarden.com/help/emergency-access/)). Use **view**
   access with a 7-day wait. It holds:
   - the minisign key and its password;
   - the Android upload key and its password;
   - the Apple credentials;
   - the Vercel and Cloudflare recovery codes;
   - the GitHub recovery codes.
2. **GitHub successor.** Tal names the second maintainer as the
   **successor** of his personal account (Settings → Account → Successor
   settings → Add successor), so that the repository can continue if the
   account cannot
   ([GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/repository-access-and-collaboration/maintaining-ownership-continuity-of-your-personal-accounts-repositories)).
3. **Security reports.** Both maintainers get every advisory. If one does not
   answer within 48 hours, the other owns it (`SECURITY.md`).
4. **A yearly drill.** Once a year, the second maintainer opens the
   emergency vault in view mode, checks that every key decrypts, and signs a
   test file with the minisign key. Then the holder rotates whatever was
   opened.

## 8. The weekly review queue

Once a week, either maintainer runs:

```sh
npm run review:queue -- --base verify/train-2 --out queue.md
```

It lists at most **five** open pull requests that change a sensitive path
and have not been human-reviewed since their last commit. They are ordered by
area (cryptography first), then by age. For each one, the queue gives:

- the sensitive files, by area;
- the questions from section 3;
- the tests in `src/__tests__` that import the changed modules;
- **attack cases** to try (a flipped ciphertext byte, a reused nonce, a
  `../` note name, `javascript:` links…);
- the commands to run.

It only reads from GitHub. Nothing is labelled or commented.

The goal is a median review time of **3 days or less**. A PR still in the
queue after a week goes first at the next sitting.

**Cryptography needs someone else.** On a PR that changes a path in the
*Cryptography* section of `.github/CODEOWNERS`, `npm run pr:check -- --pr <n>`
counts the `human-reviewed` label only when it was added by someone who is
**neither the repository owner nor the PR's author**. Tal and the agents have
written and tested that code themselves, so the point is a second person.

pages.title: Skipped tests
pages.description: Every skipped test says why, for which task and until when; npm run hygiene fails on one that does not, and npm run skips lists them all.
pages.md:
A skipped test looks like coverage but checks nothing. So every call that
skips or defers a test — `test.skip`, `it.skip`, `describe.skip`,
`*.skipIf`, `*.runIf`, `*.fixme`, `*.todo`, in `src/` (Vitest) and `e2e/`
(Playwright) — carries one structured comment, on its line or right above:

```ts
// skip-reason: <why it cannot run here> | task: <plan id or #PR> | until: YYYY-MM-DD
test.skip(dev, "the service worker runs on the production build only");
```

`npm run hygiene` (and so the Vercel preview build) fails when:

- a skip has no `skip-reason`, or it lacks the task or the date;
- the date has passed (fix the test, or justify it again with a new date) or
  is more than a year away;
- `e2e/` holds more than 15 skip calls.

## An engine gap goes through one helper

Playwright's WebKit on Linux has no Origin Private File System, so the vault
tests cannot run there. They call `vaultOrSkip(written, browserName)` from
`e2e/_opfs.ts` after seeding the vault: it skips on WebKit only, and **fails**
on Chromium and Firefox, where a vault that cannot be written is a bug — until
plan W4.12 those tests skipped quietly on every engine.

## The report

`npm run skips` prints every skip with its reason, task and date, sorted by
what it leaves out:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| engine | the flow runs on the other engines |
| setup | the flow runs only in a special setup (production build, dev server, a model or service on the machine, an opt-in measurement) |
| deferred | a `todo`: written down, checks nothing yet |

It ends with the list of vault flows WebKit does not run. `npm run skips --
--json` gives the same as JSON.
