pages.title: Every PR on the train head
pages.description: A pull request is based on the current train or on main, never on another PR's branch. pr:check warns about a stacked base and about drift, and fails an old merge base or a criss-cross. scripts/restack.mjs prints how to move a stacked PR onto the train.
pages.md:
Lumen used to stack pull requests: each PR's base was the branch of the
PR below it. By November 2026, 322 of 330 open PRs were stacked, on 175
different bases, up to 58 deep. That cost doubled histories (one branch
carried 1,398 commits of a replaced history), criss-cross merges and
about 50 hand resolutions in train 2. From now on (plan W6.22):

- **The base is the train head or `main`.** The current train is the
  highest-numbered `verify/train-N` branch on the remote
  (`verify/train-2` today). Not a `feat/*` branch, and not an older train.
- **Stay close to it.** Before the train, merge the train head into the
  branch, or restack it.
- **Stay young.** A branch whose merge base with its base is more than
  7 days old is out of date. Bring it up to date or close it.
- **The stack is at most one deep.** If your work needs another PR's
  code, wait for that PR to land in the train, then base yours on the
  train.

## What pr:check says

`npm run pr:check -- --base origin/<base>` has a section **Based on the
train head**:

| Finding | Result |
|---|---|
| The base is the current train or `main` | ok |
| The base is anything else (a stacked PR) | warning, with the restack command |
| The branch is behind its base (the train head, when stacked) | warning, with the count |
| The merge base is more than 7 days old (`--max-age-days`) | **fails** |
| More than one merge base (criss-cross) | **fails** |

`--train <branch>` names the train when the highest `verify/train-N`
isn't the one, for example while the next train is being built.

## Moving a stacked PR: scripts/restack.mjs

```bash
node scripts/restack.mjs --branch feat/my-thing --base feat/the-base
node scripts/restack.mjs --pr 412
node scripts/restack.mjs --all            # every open PR not on the train or main, parents first
```

It is a dry run. It reads git and GitHub and changes nothing. For each
PR it prints one of:

- **→ the commands.** It replays only the branch's own commits
  (`base..branch`) onto the train head, into a new branch
  `restack/<branch>`, then runs pr:check and pushes. Commits the train
  already has by patch are skipped. Merge commits are kept with
  `--rebase-merges`. Nothing is force-pushed and no PR's base changes:
  open a new PR from `restack/<branch>` that says "Supersedes #N".
- **✗ blocked.** The old base's own work isn't in the train yet, so the
  branch would lose code it builds on. Restack the base first, or wait
  for it to land in the train.
- **✓ nothing to do.** The PR is already on the train or `main`.
- **? not fetched.** Run it again with `--fetch`, or fetch the branches
  it names.

Run `--all` once a week, after the weekly train is cut, so that every PR
still open moves onto the new train.

A shallow clone can't find merge bases: deepen it first
(`git fetch --deepen=500 origin <branch>`).

pages.title: The weekly train
pages.description: How Lumen's integration trains are built, checked and promoted, every week. npm run train:build merges the PRs and resolves what it can, npm run train:status shows the ledger and the gates, and main moves at least once a week.
pages.md:
A train is an integration branch, `verify/train-N`. It starts from the
previous train's head and merges the PRs that are ready, in ascending
PR number. Vercel builds it with every gate, and once those pass, `main`
moves to it. Trains 1 and 2 were built by hand. Train 2 had 110 PRs,
and `main` didn't move for 26 days. From train 3 on (plan W6.42), the
procedure is scripted, and the train is small and weekly.

## The rules

- **At most 15 PRs per weekly train.** A catch-up train (train 3, with
  31) says so with `--max`.
- **Every PR is based on the train head** (see
  [Every PR on the train head](/contributing/train-base/)), so it merges
  without stacking.
- **At most 10 hand resolutions per train.** The ledger counts them.
- **Push the train once** when it is complete. Allow at most one fix
  push: Vercel Hobby allows 100 deployments a day.
- Every commit subject has `[skip ci]`. PR #109 (the old domain) is
  never merged. Only Tal merges into `main`.

## The week

| When (Israel time) | What | Command |
|---|---|---|
| Sunday | Cut the train: status, then build | `npm run train:status`, `npm run train:build -- --train verify/train-N --onto origin/verify/train- --from-api` |
| Sunday | Push it once. Open the train PR `verify/train-N → verify/train-` | `git push -u origin verify/train-N` |
| Monday–Tuesday | Read the Vercel result (build, budget, vitest, e2e, i18n, hygiene, docs, licences, secrets). Fix in at most one push. Run the nightly receipt on the head and the data drill | `npm run nightly -- --commit` |
| Wednesday | Lower the budgets to what the train measured (the budget ratchet, plan W6.26). Restack every PR still open onto the new train (plan W6.22) | `node scripts/budget-ratchet.mjs --sizes-log <build log> --write`, `node scripts/restack.mjs --all` |
| Thursday | Tal promotes `main` to the train when `train:status` shows every gate ✓ | — |

When a gate is still red on Thursday, the PR that breaks it leaves the
train. Rebuild the train without it (`--exclude <n>`), and it goes into
next week's train. `main` doesn't wait for one PR.

## npm run train:build

```bash
npm run train:build -- --train verify/train-3 --onto origin/verify/train-2 --prs 464-494 --max 31
npm run train:build -- --train verify/train-4 --onto origin/verify/train-3 --from-api
npm run train:build -- --continue
```

Run it in a worktree of its own. It switches to `--train`, creating it
at `--onto` if needed. Then it merges each PR with `git merge --no-ff`
and the subject `Merge #N branch [skip ci]`, skipping the ones already
in. `--prs` takes numbers and ranges, `--list` a file of "number branch"
lines, and `--from-api` every open PR whose base is the previous train
or `main`, oldest first. `--dry-run` prints the queue only. It never
pushes.

On a conflict it runs the resolver (`scripts/train/resolve.mjs`):

| File | Resolution |
|---|---|
| `i18n/keys.json` | Regenerated from the merged sources |
| Theirs' change already in ours | Ours |
| `eval/baseline/*` | Theirs |
| `*.json` | A 3-way merge per key; arrays as a union |
| Named imports on both sides | Merged per module; a removal stays removed |
| Both sides only added lines | Ours, then theirs, with the shared closing lines put back where the parser needs them |
| Both sides changed the same lines | Theirs' hunks ported onto ours (`scripts/train/port.mjs`), also into a file ours moved the code to |
| Anything else | **MANUAL**: left with diff3 markers |

Then it runs `scripts/train/check.mjs` on the TypeScript the merge
touched. That check finds parse errors, a function declared twice by a
union, unused imports, a named import a module doesn't export, and a
name declared nowhere. When the resolver or the check needs a person,
the merge stays in progress and the MANUAL lines say which files.
Resolve them by meaning (read both sides, keep both behaviours;
`git checkout --conflict=diff3 <file>` restores the markers), `git add`
them, and run `--continue`.

Each merge commit ends with a trailer, `Train-Resolution: clean`, `auto`
or `manual`, with the files. That is the ledger.

## npm run train:status

```bash
npm run train:status
npm run train:status -- --train verify/train-3 --no-api
```

It reports the current train (the highest `verify/train-N`): its head,
its age and how far it is ahead of `main`. It reports the ledger since
the previous train (clean, by the resolver, by hand; target ≤ 10 by
hand) and when `main` last moved (target: within 7 days), with the next
cut. It shows the gates of the head: the Vercel status, a nightly
receipt committed for that commit, and the data drill, which is done by
hand. It also lists the queue (open PRs on the train or `main` that it
doesn't have yet) and the median age of the open PRs it carries
(target: ≤ 7 days to `main`). A warning line names each target that is
missed.

## What the cadence is measured by

- `main` moves at least once a week, four weeks in a row.
- The median time from a PR to `main` is at most 7 days.
- At most 10 hand resolutions per weekly train.

pages.title: Translation drafts
pages.description: npm run i18n:draft drafts new UI strings in all seven languages with a local model; drafts stay "needs review" until a person approves them.
pages.md:
Lumen's interface is in eight languages. When you add an English string,
the seven others (Hebrew, Arabic, German, French, Japanese, Russian,
Simplified Chinese) need it too. Instead of leaving them empty, draft them:

```sh
npm run i18n:draft
```

The command finds every English key a language doesn't have yet, drafts it
with a model **on your machine** (Ollama), writes the drafts into
`src/i18n/locales/<lang>/<domain>.json`, and lists each one in
`i18n/needs-review/<domain>.json`. Ten new keys give seventy drafts in one
run.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--keys=a.b,c.d` | Draft only these keys |
| `--lang=he,ar` | Only these languages |
| `--model=qwen2.5:7b` | The Ollama model (`OLLAMA_HOST` sets the address, default `http://127.0.0.1:11434`) |
| `--engine=fake` | No model: writes `[he] English text` — a dry run |
| `--list` | What still needs review, per language |
| `--approve=he [--keys=…]` | Mark the Hebrew drafts (or only those keys) as reviewed |

Pass options after `--`: `npm run i18n:draft -- --keys=toolbar.save`.

## What is checked

- Every `{placeholder}` and `` `inline code` `` is swapped for a token the
  model must keep. A draft that loses, repeats or invents one is **not
  written** and is reported.
- A language that already has the key is left alone; re-running drafts
  nothing twice.

## Review

The app shows a draft right away, but the values gate
(`src/__tests__/i18nValues.test.ts`) counts every listed draft as
**untranslated**: Hebrew allows none, the other languages up to 5 %. Read
the drafts, fix what needs fixing in the locale file, then approve:

```sh
npm run i18n:draft -- --approve=he
```

Each entry in `needs-review` keeps a hash of the English text it was drafted
from, so you can tell a draft whose English changed since.

## Engines

Ollama is the engine today. The on-device translation of plan 6.4 (Chrome's
Translator, Opus-MT, M2M100) runs in the browser; it plugs in as another
engine through the same `translate(texts, lang)` interface
(`scripts/lib/i18n-draft.mjs`).

pages.title: Languages in beta, and how to help
pages.description: Six of Lumen's languages were translated by machine and are marked beta until a native speaker reviews them; suggest a better translation from inside the app.
pages.md:
Lumen's interface is in eight languages. **English** is the source and **Hebrew** is
written by native speakers. The other six were translated by machine (plan 9.1) and no
native speaker has reviewed them yet, so Lumen marks them **beta**:

| Language | Status |
|---|---|
| English | source |
| עברית (Hebrew) | native |
| العربية (Arabic) | beta |
| Русский (Russian) | beta |
| Français (French) | beta |
| Deutsch (German) | beta |
| 日本語 (Japanese) | beta |
| 简体中文 (Simplified Chinese) | beta |

In **Settings → General → Language** and in the command palette, a beta language reads
"Русский (бета)", "Français (bêta)" and so on, in the language you are using. When the
interface is in a beta language, Settings says the translation is waiting for a native
speaker's review and links to the suggestion form.

## Suggest a better translation

Command palette → **Suggest a better translation** (also linked under the language setting).

1. Type the words you saw on screen. Lumen finds the strings that contain them, in your
   language or in English.
2. Pick the string and write it the way a native speaker would. Keep every `{placeholder}`
   as it is.
3. **Open on GitHub** opens the project's new-issue form in a new tab, with the title
   (`[i18n:ru] toolbar.save`), the labels `i18n` and `locale:ru`, the English source, the
   current translation and yours. You post it with your own GitHub account. **Copy the
   text** gives you the same text to send any other way.

Nothing is sent from Lumen itself: there is no server and no account in the app. The issue
exists only once you post it.

## Review a whole language

The easiest way is in the browser, on [Weblate](/contributing/weblate/): every fix comes back as a pull request.

If you are a native speaker and want to review a whole language, the strings are in
`src/i18n/locales/<lang>/*.json`, one file per area. Open a pull request with your fixes.
New strings drafted by a model are listed in `i18n/needs-review/` until a person approves
them ([Translation drafts](/contributing/translation-drafts/)). When a language has been
reviewed, its status in `src/i18n/review.ts` changes from `beta` to `reviewed`, and the beta
mark goes away.

Arabic is Israel's second right-to-left language, so its review also covers the RTL checks
(the RTL matrix, plan 9.5, runs in Arabic too).

pages.title: Visual regression
pages.description: npm run test:visual compares ten surfaces in English and Hebrew, light and dark, with their pixel baselines — locally, no CI needed.
pages.md:
`npm run test:visual` takes 40 screenshots — ten surfaces, in English (LTR)
and Hebrew (RTL), in the light and the dark theme — and compares each with
its baseline. A pixel change nobody meant fails the run; so does a surface
without a baseline.

| Surfaces |
| --- |
| split · source · preview · WYSIWYG · command palette · keyboard shortcuts · plugin gallery · template gallery · theme settings · AI settings |

## First run on a machine

```bash
npx playwright install chromium
npm run test:visual:update      # builds, serves dist/, writes visual/__baselines__/<platform>/
```

Open every PNG, then commit the folder. From then on:

```bash
npm run test:visual
```

A failure leaves the expected, actual and diff images in `visual-results/`
(`visual-results/report/index.html`).

## What keeps the shots stable

- The production build, served by `vite preview`.
- Chromium only, 1280×800 at 1×, browser locale en-US and time zone UTC.
- A fixed note (in English or in Hebrew), a fixed clock, no service worker.
- The app's own fonts; animations, transitions, scrollbars and the caret off.
- The parts that depend on the machine (whether a local model runs) are
  masked.

Baselines are per platform: compare on the same kind of machine that wrote
them. Each shot also fails if the page is wider than the viewport — the
commonest RTL layout bug.

## An intended change

Run `npm run test:visual:update`, review the PNGs that changed and commit
them with the change.

## Does the gate work?

pages.description: Review and fix Lumen's six machine-translated languages on Hosted Weblate, in the browser, with every change coming back to the repository as a pull request.
pages.md:
Lumen's interface strings can be reviewed on **Hosted Weblate**, a translation platform
that hosts open-source projects for free. A native speaker reviews and fixes strings in
the browser. Weblate sends the changes back to the repository as a pull request, and
`npm run i18n:check` stays green on them as they are.

**Arabic comes first.** It is Israel's second right-to-left language, and its strings
were translated by machine. The brief for Arabic reviewers is
[`i18n/weblate/arabic-reviewer-brief.md`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/i18n/weblate/arabic-reviewer-brief.md).

## For translators

1. Sign in to Hosted Weblate. A GitHub account works.
2. Open the **Lumen** project and pick your language.
3. Work through the components in the order `npm run i18n:weblate -- --queue <lang>`
   prints. The startup strings come first: they are the interface before any other
   screen opens.
4. For each string, **approve** it if it reads the way a native speaker would write it,
   or fix it. Keep every `{placeholder}` exactly as it is. Weblate checks this too.

A language leaves **beta** once a native speaker has reviewed it: 100 % of the startup
strings for Arabic, and at least 50 % for each other language. Its status then changes in
`src/i18n/review.ts` (see [Languages in beta](/contributing/translations/)).

## How the sync works

| Direction | How |
|---|---|
| Repository → Weblate | Weblate reads `main` through the Hosted Weblate GitHub App. A new English string shows up after `npm run i18n:fix`, which also rewrites the English base, is merged. |
| Weblate → repository | Weblate opens a pull request with the changed `src/i18n/locales/<lang>/<domain>.json` files. A maintainer merges it once `npm run i18n:check` and `npm run i18n:weblate` pass. |

There is **one component per area** (`cmd`, `common`, `ai`, `editor`, `files`, `settings`,
`toast`, `canvas`), and each matches one locale file per language.

The setup lives in `i18n/weblate/config.json`. `npm run i18n:weblate -- --print` prints
the settings to enter in Weblate. Three choices in it matter:

- **The English base is `i18n/weblate/en/<area>.json`**, not `src/i18n/locales/en/`. The
  app ships the English strings of lazily loaded screens apart from the startup set, but
  every other language keeps both in one file. Weblate's cleanup add-on keeps only the
  keys of the base, so a base without the lazy strings would delete their translations.
  `node scripts/weblate.mjs --write` builds the base from both, and `npm run i18n:fix` runs
  it.
- **JSON as the layout writes it**: the "JSON file" format with the parameters
  `json_indent: 2`, `json_sort_keys: case_sensitive`, spaces, and no compact separators.
  Weblate writes JSON with translate-toolkit, which uses Python's `json.dumps` with
  `ensure_ascii` off and a newline at the end. With these parameters, every one of the 56
  translation files comes out byte for byte the same. All keys are ASCII, so Python's sort
  and JavaScript's agree.
- **The "Remove blank strings" add-on.** The UI shows an empty translation as empty: `""`
  does not fall back to English. `npm run i18n:weblate` refuses an empty value.

## For the maintainer: setting it up once

1. Request libre hosting on Hosted Weblate for the public `talstilkol/lumen-md`
   repository (MIT). Weblate's free hosting is for projects with a licence that OSI
   approves or the FSF recognises as libre, whose source is public.
2. Install the **Hosted Weblate GitHub App** on `talstilkol/lumen-md` only.
3. Create the project `lumen-md` and the 8 components from `npm run i18n:weblate -- --print`.
   Turn on reviews, and add the two cleanup add-ons.
4. Ask the Arabic reviewers to start, with the brief.

pages.title: Accessibility statement
pages.description: How accessible Lumen is — the standard it follows (Israeli Standard 5568, WCAG), what works, known gaps, and how to report a barrier.
pages.md:
This statement covers the Lumen app (web, desktop and mobile builds) at
version **0.1.0**. It was last reviewed on **10 November 2026** and is
updated with every release: a test (`a11yStatement.test.ts`) fails the
build when the version here and the app's version differ.

## Standard

Israel's Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities regulations (service
accessibility adjustments, regulation 35) require **Israeli Standard
5568**, which adopts **WCAG 2.0 level AA**. Lumen aims for **WCAG 2.2
level AA**, which includes everything WCAG 2.0 AA asks for.

## What is accessible

- **Keyboard:** every feature is a command in the palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K).
  Dialogs keep focus, Escape closes them, and focus returns to where it was.
- **Screen readers:** dialogs, the editor, the palette and the sidebar edge
  have names and roles. The editor speaks the structure of the line the
  cursor lands on (heading and level, task and its state, code block,
  quote), new suggestions, and the start and end of long AI work. It speaks
  in the interface language, Hebrew or English. **Announce cursor position**
  gives the line, the column and the heading above. **Screen reader
  announcements** switches between headings and structure (default), every
  line, and off.
- **Right-to-left:** Hebrew lines read right to left and English lines left
  to right, in the same document.
- **Contrast:** text is at least 4.5:1 in light and dark mode.
- **Zoom and reflow:** at 200 % and 400 % zoom the main screen, the side
  panels and the dialogs fit the window without scrolling sideways. Code
  blocks scroll inside their own box.
- **High contrast:** in Windows high-contrast mode (forced colours), focus,
  buttons and selected items use the system colours.
- **Reduced motion:** with the system setting on, animations and smooth
  scrolling stop.

## How it is checked

- axe-core (WCAG 2.0/2.1 A and AA) on six surfaces, in Hebrew and English,
  in light and dark mode (`e2e/a11y.spec.ts`).
- In every preview build, axe-core (WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 A and AA, target
  size included) on the key Hebrew flows: the main screen in source and
  preview, the calendar and ten dialogs, light and dark
  (`e2e/a11y-hebrew-gate.spec.ts`), and the Hebrew accessibility tree
  (`e2e/aria-hebrew.spec.ts`). A serious or critical violation fails the
  build.
- The same axe rules on 52 of the app's panels and dialogs rendered on
  their own, in Hebrew (light and dark) and English.
- The Hebrew journey under VoiceOver, scripted with Guidepup, on the nightly
  Mac ([screen readers, automated](/editor/screen-reader-automation/)).
- Reflow at 320 px and 640 px wide on ten surfaces, plus a forced-colours
  focus check (`e2e/reflow.spec.ts`).
- Spoken announcements (`e2e/sr-announce.spec.ts`).
- A fixed journey in Hebrew with NVDA, VoiceOver (macOS and iOS) and
  TalkBack: the [screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/).

## Known gaps

The [accessibility conformance report](/editor/acr/) lists every WCAG 2.2
level A and AA criterion with its status, and a remediation plan for each
one that is only partly met. In short:

- The screen-reader journey has not yet been run with all three screen
  readers for this version. The results are recorded in the protocol when
  it is.
- Charts, diagrams (Mermaid, Graphviz), the canvas and the map are
  pictures. Their source text in the note is the accessible version.
- Content you write yourself, such as images without alt text, is yours to
  make accessible. The alt-text helper can suggest descriptions.

## Accessibility coordinator

Lumen is an open-source project. Its maintainer is its accessibility
coordinator: write through the form below, or open the issue in Hebrew.
Each report gets a reply with what will be done and when.

## Report a barrier

Use the [accessibility report form](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues/new?template=accessibility.yml)
(it is labelled **accessibility**), or **Report an accessibility problem**
in the command palette. Say what you were doing, which screen reader or
tool you used, and what happened. You can write in Hebrew or English.
Accessibility reports are triaged before other bugs.

pages.description: Keyboard use, screen readers, contrast and reduced motion in Lumen — and how each is checked.
pages.md:
Lumen is meant to be used without a mouse, with a screen reader, in Hebrew
or English, in light or dark mode.

## Keyboard

- **⌘K / Ctrl+K** opens the command palette; every feature is a command
  there. **⌘/ / Ctrl+/** lists the shortcuts.
- **Dialogs keep focus.** When a dialog opens, focus moves into it. Tab
  and Shift+Tab stay inside it, **Escape** closes it, and focus returns to
  where it was before (for example the editor). This holds for every modal
  dialog: the palette, search, settings, prompts, setup, version history,
  sign-in, sync conflicts and the rest.
- **The sidebar's edge** is a separator you can reach with Tab. **←/→**
  resize the sidebar by 16 px (**Shift**: 48 px), **Home** / **End** make it
  narrowest / widest. In right-to-left layouts the arrows follow the edge's
  direction.
- The command list in the palette can be reached with Tab and scrolled with
  the keyboard.

## Screen readers

Dialogs are announced with their names (`role="dialog"`, `aria-modal`, a
label). The editor has a label, the palette is a combobox with a listbox,
and the sidebar edge reports its width (`aria-valuenow`).

In the editor, moving the cursor onto a heading, a task, a code fence or a
quote speaks what it is ("Heading 2: Plan", "Task, done"), in the interface
language. A new suggestion and long AI work (when it starts and when it
ends) are spoken too. From the palette:

- **Announce cursor position**: the line, the column and the heading above.
- **Screen reader announcements**: switch between headings and structure
  (the default), every line, and off.

See the [accessibility statement](/editor/accessibility-statement/) and the
[screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/).

## Contrast

Text meets WCAG AA (at least 4.5:1) in light and dark mode: the accent
colour, muted text, inline code and the status-bar indicators (saved,
warning, error) were adjusted for this.

## Reduced motion

With the system's *reduce motion* setting on, animations and transitions are
cut to an instant, and scrolling that Lumen starts (the outline, comments,
typewriter mode, page view) jumps instead of gliding.

## How it is checked

- `e2e/a11y.spec.ts` runs [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core)
  (WCAG 2.0/2.1 A and AA rules, colour contrast included) on the main
  screen, the command palette, search, the shortcuts list, theme settings and
  setup — in English (left-to-right) and Hebrew (right-to-left), light and
  dark. Any *serious* or *critical* finding fails the build.
- The same file walks a keyboard-only path: palette, a dialog that keeps
  focus for 25 Tab presses and gives it back, and the sidebar edge.
- `src/__tests__/useFocusTrap.test.tsx` covers the shared focus trap.

<!-- Generated by scripts/acr.mjs from docs/acr/wcag22.json — edit that file. -->

This report follows the structure of the VPAT® 2.5 (WCAG edition). It covers **Lumen 0.1.0** (web, desktop and mobile) against **WCAG 2.2** levels A and AA, and was last reviewed on **2026-11-10**. It is published again with every major release: `node scripts/acr.mjs --check` fails when the report's version and the app's differ.

## Summary

| Level | Supports | Partially supports | Does not support | Not applicable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 22 | 5 | 0 | 4 |
| AA | 16 | 6 | 0 | 2 |

## How it was evaluated

Automated: axe-core on six surfaces in Hebrew and English, light and dark (e2e/a11y.spec.ts); reflow at 320 and 640 px and forced colours (e2e/reflow.spec.ts); spoken announcements (e2e/sr-announce.spec.ts); unit tests of the focus trap, contrast and toasts. Manual: review of each criterion against the app's code and behaviour for this version.

## Level A

| Criterion | Status | Remarks |
|---|---|---|
| [1.1.1 Non-text Content](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-content) | Partially supports | Icons and icon buttons have text names (axe). Charts, diagrams, the canvas and maps drawn from note text are pictures: their alternative is the source text in the note, which is always one click away, but the picture itself has no text alternative. **Plan:** Give chart and diagram blocks a text summary (title, series, values) as their accessible name, and the canvas an outline of its shapes. (0.2.0) |
| [1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/audio-only-and-video-only-prerecorded) | Not applicable | Lumen's own interface has no prerecorded audio or video. Media in notes is the author's content. |
| [1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/captions-prerecorded) | Not applicable | No prerecorded media with sound in the interface. |
| [1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/audio-description-or-media-alternative-prerecorded) | Not applicable | No prerecorded video in the interface. |
| [1.3.1 Info and Relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/info-and-relationships) | Supports | Dialogs, menus, the palette (combobox + listbox), tabs, tables and forms use native elements or ARIA roles with names. In the editor, the structure of the line under the cursor (heading level, task state, code block, quote) is spoken. |
| [1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/meaningful-sequence) | Supports | The reading order follows the DOM order in both directions; Hebrew and English runs are isolated so they read in their own direction. |
| [1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/sensory-characteristics) | Supports | Instructions name the control ("the Settings button", "⌘K"), never only its shape, colour or place. |
| [1.4.1 Use of Color](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color) | Partially supports | Messages, errors and selections carry text or a named icon as well as colour (axe's colour rules pass on six surfaces). In the status bar, the sync and collaboration indicators show their state by icon and colour, with the words only in a tooltip. **Plan:** Status-bar indicators with a visible word ("Synced", "Offline") and an accessible name, translated (their tooltips are English-only today). (0.2.0) |
| [1.4.2 Audio Control](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/audio-control) | Supports | Nothing plays sound on its own. Read-aloud starts on request and has a stop control. |
| [2.1.1 Keyboard](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/keyboard) | Partially supports | Every feature is a command in the palette, dialogs keep and return focus, the sidebar edge resizes with arrow keys. The canvas whiteboard (tldraw) and the map can be panned and zoomed with the keyboard, but drawing new shapes needs a pointer. **Plan:** Keyboard commands to add, move and connect shapes on the canvas. (0.2.0) |
| [2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/no-keyboard-trap) | Supports | Tab in the editor indents (as in every code editor); pressing Escape and then Tab moves focus out (CodeMirror's behaviour). Dialogs release focus on Escape. |

pages.title: Arabic (beta)
pages.description: Write Arabic next to Hebrew and English in one note. Each line takes its own direction, tashkeel can be hidden or removed, search ignores it, and Arabic spelling runs on this device.
pages.md:
Lumen treats Arabic the way it treats Hebrew. Arabic is still marked
**beta** in the language picker: the interface strings were machine-translated
and wait for a native speaker's review ([help translate](../../contributing/translations/)).

## Arabic, Hebrew and English in one note

Each paragraph, heading, list, quote and table cell takes the direction of its
own first letter. An Arabic paragraph runs right to left, the English one under
it left to right, and a Hebrew one right to left. This works the same in the
editor, the preview, WYSIWYG and the exports. Code always runs left to right,
even with an Arabic comment.

## Tashkeel

- **Hide or show Arabic tashkeel** (`⌘K`) hides the harakat, tanwin, shadda
  and sukun in the editor and keeps the letters. The note keeps every mark:
  copying, saving and exporting are not affected. Run the command again to
  show them.
- **Remove Arabic tashkeel (selection or note)** removes the marks from the
  selection, or from the whole note when nothing is selected. It is one change,
  so `⌘Z` brings them back.

## Search

Search ignores tashkeel and tatweel, and treats the spellings writers use
interchangeably as the same: أ إ آ and ا, ى and ي, ة and ه. A search for

pages.title: Citations with [@key]
pages.description: Cite from your BibTeX, CSL-JSON or Zotero library with pandoc's [@key, p. 10], in APA, Chicago, MLA or the Israeli APA, with a reference list in the preview, DOCX and PDF.
pages.md:
## Cite in two keystrokes

Press `⌥⌘C` (or `⌘K → "Insert a citation [@key]…"`) to open the cite
dialog. It searches your whole library at once.

- With nothing typed, the sources you cited last come first: **Enter**
  cites the last one again, and **↓ Enter** the one before it.
- Type to search by author, title, year or key. Hebrew works.
- **Tab** goes to the locator field (`p. 10`, `chap. 3`, `עמ׳ 12`).
- **Enter** writes `[@key]`. **⇧Enter** writes `@key`, for a citation
  inside the sentence.

## Your library

The library is everything in the vault, read on this device:

- **BibTeX**: any `*.bib` file.
- **CSL-JSON**: `*.csl.json`, `references.json` or `bibliography.json`
  (Zotero, Zettlr and pandoc all export this format).
- **Zotero**: in the desktop app, run `⌘K → "Citations: copy the Zotero
  library into the vault"`, or press **Copy from Zotero** in the dialog.
  This copies Zotero 7's library from this computer into
  `.lumen/zotero-library.csl.json` (first turn on Settings → Advanced →
  "Allow other applications on this computer to communicate with Zotero").

Keys come from the source: the BibTeX key, CSL's `citation-key`, or a
`Citation Key:` line from Better BibTeX. Otherwise the key is the author's
family name and the year (`austen1813`, `כהן2020`).

## Zotero without the desktop app

On the web and on phones, **⌘K → Citations: sync the Zotero library from
zotero.org (read-only)** reads your library from Zotero's Web API. Zotero
Desktop doesn't need to be open.

1. On zotero.org, open **Settings → Security → Applications** and create a
   key with **read-only** access to your library.
2. Run the command and paste the key. It is kept in this device's secret
   store and sent only to `api.zotero.org`, as the `Zotero-API-Key` header.
   Every request shows in the privacy ledger as a cloud route. A
   **local-only** AI and privacy policy blocks it.
3. Your sources join the cite dialog, the same as the desktop copy. Items
   with notes or PDFs also get a note in `Zotero/`, headed with their
   `[@key]`. The note holds the Zotero notes as Markdown, a link that opens
   each PDF in Zotero, and a link to it on zotero.org.

The next sync asks only for what changed since the last one. If nothing
changed, Zotero answers with one empty response (`304`). Otherwise Lumen
fetches the changed items, up to 50 per request, and drops the deleted ones.
The sync itself never writes to Zotero; the one write is
[sending PDF highlights](/workspace/pdf-reader/#send-highlights-to-zotero),
after you confirm it, with a key that has write access. If Zotero asks the app to slow down
(`Backoff`, `429`), Lumen waits.

## Pandoc syntax

| You write | APA 7 shows |
|---|---|
| `[@austen1813]` | (Austen, 1813) |
| `[@austen1813, p. 10]` | (Austen, 1813, p. 10) |
| `[see @austen1813, pp. 10–12; @darwin1859]` | (see Austen, 1813, pp. 10–12; Darwin, 1859) |
| `[-@austen1813]` | (1813) |
| `@austen1813 [p. 10] writes` | Austen (1813, p. 10) writes |

Locators can be pages, chapters, sections, figures, volumes, paragraphs,
notes or lines, in English or Hebrew. Chicago writes the page bare
(`(Austen 1813, 10)`), and so does MLA (`(Austen 10)`).

A key the library doesn't know stays as you wrote it.

## Styles

Set the style in the note's frontmatter:

```yaml
---
citation-style: il      # apa (default), chicago, mla, il
---
```

- **APA 7**, **Chicago author-date** and **MLA 9** use the 6.13 templates,
  in the note's language (Hebrew notes get ו, ואחרים, עמ׳).
- **il** is APA 7 the way Israeli academic libraries teach it:
  - Hebrew sources come first, in their own list, then the rest.
  - Each source is written in its own language.
  - Hebrew initials take a geresh: `דרשן, ד׳`.
  - The same author and year are told apart by א / ב (a / b for other
    languages).

The reference list goes where the note has pandoc's `::: {#refs}` block,
or at the end of the note. It appears in the preview, when you print to
PDF and in **Export to Word**.

All formatting is the app's own, with no citeproc and nothing fetched.

pages.title: Direction marks (bidi)
pages.description: See the invisible characters that set text direction, clean the ones that do nothing, fix reversed brackets, and catch Trojan Source text.
pages.md:
Hebrew and Arabic text pasted from a word processor, a web page or a chat
app often carries characters you cannot see. They set the direction of the
text around them, and they are the usual reason a pasted paragraph suddenly
runs the wrong way or a bracket jumps to the other end of the line. Lumen
shows them, removes the ones that do nothing, and warns you about the
dangerous ones.

## Show direction marks

Command palette (⌘K) → **Show direction marks**. Every direction control
gets a small tag in front of it, in the source editor and in WYSIWYG:

| Tag | Name | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LRM` `RLM` `ALM` | left-to-right, right-to-left, Arabic letter mark | an invisible letter of that direction; pins a line that starts with a number or a Latin word |
| `LRE` `RLE` … `PDF` | embeddings | lay out the text up to `PDF` in that direction |
| `LRO` `RLO` … `PDF` | overrides | force every character up to `PDF` into that order, even Hebrew letters |
| `LRI` `RLI` `FSI` … `PDI` | isolates | lay out a run (a URL, a name) on its own, without disturbing the line |

The character stays where it is, so the line lays out exactly as it does
anywhere else. The tag only shows you why. Run the command again to hide the
tags. The setting is kept on this device.

## Clean direction marks and fix brackets

Command palette → **Clean direction marks and fix brackets** does two things
as **one** change, so a single Undo (⌘Z) brings everything back:

- **Removes marks that change nothing on screen.** These are decided by the
  Unicode bidi algorithm (UAX #9), not guessed:
  - an `RLM` right before a Hebrew letter, or right after one;
  - an `LRM` right before or right after a Latin letter;
  - an `ALM` right after an Arabic letter;
  - an embedding or isolate with nothing inside;
  - a `PDF` or `PDI` that closes nothing.

  A mark that does change the display stays. Examples are the `RLM` in front
  of `10:30 פגישה`, an `LRM` after a number, and an `RLM` after Arabic text,
  which changes how the digits after it are read. Overrides always stay too.
- **Swaps brackets typed backwards in right-to-left lines.** `)טקסט(` was
  typed that way so it would look right in a program that did not handle
  direction. When every bracket of one kind in a line is backwards, and
  swapping them balances the line, they are swapped. Smileys (`:)`), list
  numbers (`1)`), links and left-to-right lines are left alone.

Fenced code and code spans are never changed.

## The paste warning (Trojan Source)

Two things make text display in an order other than the one it is stored in:

- an **override** (`LRO`, `RLO`);
- an embedding or isolate **left open** at the end of its line.

What you read is then not what a search, a diff or a compiler sees. This is
the "Trojan Source" attack (CVE-2021-42574).

Lumen tags these characters in **red** whether or not the marks are shown.
When you paste or drop text that contains them, a warning appears with a
**Remove them** button. The button deletes only those characters, as one
undoable change, so the text displays in the order it is stored. Harmless
isolates and marks stay.

## Limits

- **Lines are checked one at a time.** An isolate opened on one line and
  closed on the next counts as left open, as it does in the browser.
- **Only these 12 controls are covered.** Zero-width joiners and
  non-joiners are not direction controls and are not shown.

pages.title: Handwriting and ink
pages.description: Write or draw with a pen, an Apple Pencil, a finger or a mouse inside a note. The ink is saved as SVG in the Markdown file, so the note still opens in Obsidian and other editors.
pages.md:
Lumen lets you write by hand inside a note: a sketch next to lecture notes,
a formula you would rather draw than type, a signature, a diagram.

## Draw

1. Put the cursor where the ink should go.
2. Open the command palette and run **Handwriting: draw or edit**.
3. Write on the pad. Lift the pen and write again; every stroke is kept.
4. Press **Insert**.

The pad has a **pen** and an **eraser**, four colours, three widths,
**Undo** (also Ctrl+Z / ⌘Z) and **Clear**.

- **Pen and Apple Pencil:** the line gets wider as you press harder.
- **Finger and mouse:** Lumen has no pressure to read, so it estimates the
  width from your speed.
- **The eraser end of a pen** erases, without choosing the eraser first.
  The eraser removes whole strokes.

### Palm rejection

While the pen touches the screen, and for half a second after you lift it,
a hand resting on the screen draws nothing. A stroke that the palm started
just before the pen touched down is thrown away.

Once you have used a pen on the pad, fingers stop drawing, as in most note
apps. To draw with a finger again, turn on **Draw with a finger**. Two fingers
on the pad never draw.

## Where the ink sits

- **On its own line** (the default): at the start of the line. In a Hebrew
  or Arabic note that is the right-hand edge; in an English note, the left.
- **Beside the text (study page)**: the ink floats at the end of the line,
  and the paragraph after it flows around it. In a Hebrew note it sits on the
  left of the text. Use it for handwritten margin notes next to printed text.

Lumen takes the direction from the paragraph just before the cursor, so the
ink is placed the same way in every reader.

## Edit or remove

- In the preview, **double-click** the ink.
- In the source editor, put the cursor anywhere inside the ink block and run
  **Handwriting: draw or edit** again.

Save keeps the ink where it was. Clear and then Save removes it from the note,
with its blank lines.

## What is in the file

The ink is an SVG image written into the Markdown:

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" data-lumen-ink="1" data-ink-id="k3f9a2xq" data-ink-dir="rtl" data-ink-place="block" viewBox="0 0 189 175" width="189" height="175" role="img" aria-label="Handwriting" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto;margin-left:auto">
<path fill="#1f2937" d="M64.3,21.6 Q69.2,25.6 …Z" data-ink-size="5" data-ink-pts="63,23,0.3 67,26.9,0.31 …"/>
</svg>
```

- It is an **HTML block** in Markdown terms: a blank line before and after it,
  and none inside it. The note stays valid Markdown.
- **Obsidian** (reading view) and other editors that show inline HTML draw the
  ink as it looks in Lumen. Editors that hide inline HTML, and GitHub, leave
  the text around it unchanged.
- Each `<path>` keeps the pen points (`data-ink-pts`: x, y and pressure), so
  Lumen can open the ink again for editing. Saving an ink without changing it
  writes back the same bytes.
- Nothing leaves your device: the pad and the ink need no network.

## Limits

- The eraser removes whole strokes, not parts of one.
- Handwriting recognition (turning Hebrew handwriting into text) is not part
  of this feature yet.
- An ink you write by hand in SVG, without `data-ink-pts`, is shown and kept,
  but its strokes cannot be erased in the pad.

pages.description: Definitions, synonyms and the niqqud of a word, from Hebrew Wiktionary, offline inside the editor.
pages.md:
Right-click a Hebrew word in the editor to see its **synonyms**, its **definition** or its
**niqqud**. Everything is looked up on this device, from a dictionary pack you download once.

## Get the dictionary

Command palette (**⌘K / Ctrl+K**) → **Hebrew dictionary and synonyms (download / remove)**.
Lumen shows the pack's size, its number of entries and its licence, and downloads it only
after you agree. The pack comes from Lumen's own site and is checked against its published
size and checksum. It is kept in the browser's storage, so it works offline. Run the same
command again to remove it.

## Use it

- **Right-click** a Hebrew word: **Synonyms**, **Definition**, **Niqqud of the word**.
  **Shift+right-click** opens the browser's own menu (copy, paste, spelling).
- Or put the cursor on the word and run **Look up the Hebrew word at the cursor**.
- Prefix letters are understood: **ובבית** finds **בית**. A synonym you click replaces the
  word and keeps its prefix (**ובבית** → **ובדירה**). The pointed form replaces the word the
  same way; the prefix letters stay unpointed.
- Text with niqqud is looked up without it.
- Synonyms go both ways: if one entry lists another word as a synonym, that word shows the
  first one too.

Nothing changes in the note until you pick a word, and then only that word, if it is
still there.

## Where the words come from

The pack is built from the **Hebrew Wiktionary** (he.wiktionary.org), whose text is licensed
**CC BY-SA 4.0**. For each entry it keeps the pointed headword, the part of speech, up to
four definitions (shortened, without examples) and the synonyms section. The credit is in
**Credits** (command palette) and in the dictionary window, and the pack ships with its
licence (`public/lexicon/LICENSE.md`).

**Why Wiktionary, not Hspell:** Hspell's word lists are AGPL-3.0, which cannot ship inside
Lumen (MIT). Lumen's spelling checker still offers Hspell as a separate download from its
upstream. Wiktionary's CC BY-SA licence applies to the pack, which is a separate file, not
to Lumen's code.

## Build the pack (maintainers)

```bash
curl -LO https://dumps.wikimedia.org/hewiktionary/latest/hewiktionary-latest-pages-articles.xml.bz2
npm run lexicon:build -- hewiktionary-latest-pages-articles.xml.bz2 20261101
```

This writes `public/lexicon/he-wiktionary.json` and `public/lexicon/manifest.json` (size,
sha256, entry count). Commit both; the app offers the download once the manifest exists.

pages.title: Hebrew grammar and style
pages.description: Hebrew grammar and style checks that run on this device, beyond spelling, with three writing levels and a short explanation for each suggestion.
pages.md:
With grammar checking on (`⌘K` → **Enable grammar check (LanguageTool)**), Hebrew
paragraphs are checked on this device. Nothing is sent anywhere. Each
suggestion comes with a one-line explanation.

## What it catches

| Error | Example | Suggestion |
|---|---|---|
| Number and gender (3–10) | שלוש ילדים | שלושה ילדים |
| Two before a noun | שתי ספרים, שניים ילדים | שני ספרים, שני ילדים |
| הכי with ביותר | הכי טוב ביותר | טוב ביותר |
| את instead of עם | נפגשתי את דני | נפגשתי עם דני |
| The article in a construct pair | הבית ספר | בית הספר |
| אני with a third-person future | אני ילך | אני אלך |
| A repeated meaning | חזר שוב, בערך כמאה | חזר, כמאה |

The rules are careful rather than greedy. If the word list cannot tell a
noun's gender, the noun is left alone, and so are compound numbers like
שלוש עשרה.

## Writing levels

`⌘K` → **Hebrew grammar: change the writing level** cycles through three
levels:

- **Everyday:** only the errors in the table above.
- **Academic** and **Legal:** also flag spoken Hebrew in formal writing, such
  as הכי חשוב (→ חשוב ביותר) and בגלל ש (→ מכיוון ש).

## A local model (optional)

The rules never need a model. If you want one, a model running in Ollama
on this computer (DictaLM 3.0 1.7B, for example) can judge each grammar
suggestion and drop the ones it rejects. The checker talks to `localhost`
only.

## How it is measured

`eval/probes/hebrew-grammar.json` has 200 sentences with one marked error
each, and the corrected sentence beside each one.
`src/__tests__/hebrewGrammar.test.ts` checks four things:
- that at least 70% of the errors are found;
- that at most 5% of the corrected sentences, and of the 1,302 sentences of
  real prose in the HeQ dev paragraphs, get any suggestion;
- the time per paragraph;
- that no request is made.

The probe was written for this repository, so its numbers are development
numbers. A held-out set of real sentences with marked errors is still
needed.

pages.title: Hebrew keyboard layout
pages.description: Shortcuts that work with the Hebrew layout on, and search that understands text typed with the wrong layout.
pages.md:
## Shortcuts work in any layout

Lumen reads a shortcut by the **key you press**, not by the letter it types.
With the Hebrew layout on, **Ctrl+K** (⌘K) still opens the palette, even
though that key types ל. The same holds for every shortcut: save, open, new,
the editor modes (⌘1–⌘4), find and replace, the shortcuts list (⌘/), undo,
redo and the rest.

With the Hebrew layout active, the shortcuts list (⌘/ / Ctrl+/) shows the
Hebrew letter on each key too: **Ctrl+K (ל)**. Lumen knows the layout from
what you last typed, or from the interface language if you haven't typed yet.

**AltGr** (Ctrl+Alt on Windows) never triggers a shortcut. Characters typed
with AltGr stay characters.

## Typed with the wrong layout

`akuo` is `שלום` typed with the English layout on, and `יקךךם` is `hello`
typed with the Hebrew one. The **command palette** and **workspace search**
read your text both ways:

- The palette shows matches for what you typed first, then matches for the
  other-layout reading, with a note: *Also showing results for “חיפוש”*.
- Search tries the other reading when what you typed finds fewer than three
  notes.

Only text in a single script is converted. Mixed Hebrew and English is taken
as you typed it.

## How it is checked

`src/__tests__/keyboardLayout.test.ts`:

- 50 golden wrong-layout queries (25 each way) must find the right command in
  the top 3, in at least 95% of cases.
- Every shortcut is checked with the English layout, the Hebrew layout and
  macOS ⌘.
- No two shortcuts may share a key, and every shortcut the palette shows must
  be the one the app binds.

`e2e/hebrew-layout.spec.ts` presses the shortcuts as the Hebrew layout sends
them.

pages.title: Hebrew and right-to-left
pages.description: How Lumen decides the direction of every block — paragraphs, tables, lists, quotes and code — in the editor, the preview, WYSIWYG and the export.
pages.md:
Lumen doesn't make a whole note right-to-left or left-to-right. Each block
reads in the direction of **its own** text, so a Hebrew paragraph sits on
the right and the English one after it on the left, in the same note.

| Block | Direction |
| --- | --- |
| Paragraph, heading | Its first strong letter (Hebrew → right-to-left) |
| List, list item, quote | Its own text: a Hebrew list has its markers and indent on the right, its quote bar on the right |
| Table (preview, export) | The table left-to-right; **each cell** by its own text |
| Table (WYSIWYG) | Each cell's paragraph by its own text |
| Code, math | Always left-to-right, even with a Hebrew comment |

The same rules apply in the source editor (line by line), the preview,
WYSIWYG and the HTML export — an exported Hebrew note opens as
`<html lang="he" dir="rtl">` with the same `dir` on every block.

## The workspace in Hebrew

With the interface in Hebrew, the whole workspace is mirrored, the way
Obsidian does it: the toolbar and the status bar start on the right, the
file tree sits on the right and the outline and backlinks on the left,
tabs run from right to left, menus open from their button's right edge,
and floating controls (the AI button, find & replace, notifications) sit
on the left. The source editor and code stay left-to-right.

The arrow keys keep their visual meaning: **←** moves to what is drawn on
the left. In the Hebrew tab strip that is the next tab; in the welcome tour
← is "next". Home and End go to the first and the last tab.

## Tested

`e2e/rtl-matrix.spec.ts` checks tables, bulleted, numbered, nested and task
lists, quotes and code in the preview, WYSIWYG and the export, with the
interface in Hebrew and in English, in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and on
an iPhone 14 and a Pixel 7. `visual/rtl.visual.ts` keeps pixel baselines of
the same note (see [Visual regression](/contributing/visual-regression/)).

`e2e/rtl-parity.spec.ts` checks 20 workspace scenarios in both interface
languages and runs axe on the Hebrew workspace; `src/__tests__/rtlLogical.test.ts`
fails when app CSS, an inline style or a Tailwind class uses a physical
left / right instead of the logical start / end.

pages.title: Hebrew typography
pages.description: Gershayim, geresh, maqaf, Hebrew quotation marks and numbers, fixed as you type or for a whole note. Each rule can be turned off.
pages.md:
Word has fixed Hebrew punctuation automatically for decades. In Lumen, the
source editor does the same **as you type**, and **Hebrew typography…** in
the command palette applies it to a whole note after a preview.

| Rule | You type | You get |
|---|---|---|
| Gershayim | `צה"ל` | צה״ל |
| Geresh | `ג'ירפה` | ג׳ירפה |
| Hebrew quotation marks | `"שלום"` | „שלום” |
| Maqaf | `בית-ספר` | בית־ספר |
| Dash between words | `אחד - שניים` | אחד – שניים |
| Numbers | `50 %`, `%50`, `10–20` | 50%, 50%, 10-20 (a range reads in order right to left) |
| Mixed lines | `HTML היא שפה.` | an invisible right-to-left mark (RLM) at the start, so the line reads right to left and the period lands at its end |

Every rule works only in a Hebrew context. `say "hello"`, `it's` and `ב-2026`
stay as they are, and so does a prefix before a quote: `ו"ההגנה"` becomes
ו„ההגנה”, not a gershayim.

## Never changed

Nothing changes inside **code** (fenced blocks and inline code), **links**
and URLs, wiki-links, HTML tags, math, or the **frontmatter**.

## Undo

Each fix is its own undo step. **Ctrl+Z / ⌘Z** right after a fix gives back
the character you typed, and the next keys you type don't redo the fix. A
quotation mark right after a Hebrew letter is fixed when you type the next
key, because by then it is clear whether it is ״ (צה"ל) or a closing ”.

## Turning rules off

In **Hebrew typography…** (command palette):

- **Fix as I type** turns the automatic fixes on or off.
- Each rule has its own checkbox.
- The dialog lists every change the rules would make to the current note.
  **Apply to the note** makes them all as one undo step.

The settings are saved in this browser.

## How it is checked

`src/__tests__/hebrewTypography.test.ts` covers:

- 50 golden cases.
- A note with code, links, URLs, HTML, math and frontmatter where none of
  those change.
- Each rule turned off on its own.
- Typing character by character, including an undone fix that stays undone.

`e2e/hebrew-typography.spec.ts` types in the editor, undoes a fix, and
applies the dialog.

pages.title: Hebrew and right-to-left
pages.description: Writing in Hebrew (and Arabic) in Lumen — direction per line, the interface in Hebrew, search that ignores niqqud and prefixes, spelling on this device, and exports that keep the direction.
pages.md:
Lumen is built for notes that mix Hebrew and English.

## The interface

`⌘K → Language: …` switches the interface. Hebrew and Arabic flip the
whole layout (sidebar, menus and dialogs mirror). The interface is in 8
languages: English, Hebrew, Arabic, Russian, French, German, Japanese and
Chinese.

## Direction in a note

- **Per line, automatically.** In the source editor each line takes its
  direction from its first strong letter: a Hebrew paragraph aligns right,
  an English one left, and the cursor and selection follow. Code blocks
  and the front matter are always left-to-right.
- **For a whole note:** put `dir: rtl` (or `ltr`) in its front matter.
- **For the editor:** `⌘K → Text Direction: RTL (Right to Left)` (and back
  with *Text Direction: LTR*).

## Search

Workspace search folds niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix
letters ו ה ב כ ל מ ש, so *בבית*, *והבית* and *הַבַּיִת* all find *בית*.
The exact form ranks first. See
[Workspace search](/workspace/search/). Links between notes and heading
anchors compare names the same way, so `[[שלום]]` finds *שָׁלוֹם.md*.

## Spelling, on this device

Hebrew paragraphs are checked **locally**: a final letter inside a word, a
repeated word, a space before punctuation. For spelling against a
dictionary, download Hspell's word list once with
`⌘K → Hebrew spelling: dictionary (download / remove)` (5.7 MB). It
is AGPL-3.0, so it isn't bundled; it is stored on this device, and the
same command removes it. Turn the check on with
`⌘K → Enable grammar check (LanguageTool)`. **Hebrew text never goes to
LanguageTool**: only paragraphs that are mostly Latin are sent, with any
Hebrew words in them blanked out.

## Exports

Exports keep the direction: Word (.docx) marks Hebrew paragraphs and runs
as right-to-left, and an exported HTML file opens right-to-left when the
note is Hebrew (or its front matter says `dir: rtl`).

pages.title: Legal citations (Israel)
pages.description: Rulings, laws, bills, books and articles by the Israeli uniform citation rules, and a citation from a case number in the note.
pages.md:
Lumen writes legal citations by **כללי האזכור האחיד בכתיבה המשפטית**, the third edition
(Tel Aviv University Faculty of Law, February 2021), which most Israeli law reviews and
faculties follow. Academic sources outside law use the
[Israeli APA style](/editor/citations/) ("APA 7 — Israeli academic").

## Insert a legal citation

Command palette → **Citations: legal source (uniform citation rules)…**. Choose the kind of
source, fill in the fields, and the citation is written as you type. **Insert** puts it at
the cursor, as plain text in the note, so it reads the same in the preview, in print and in
a DOCX or PDF export.

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Supreme Court, printed | `בג"ץ 7/48 אל-כרבוטלי נ' שר-הבטחון, פ"ד ב 5, פס' 14 (1949).` |
| Lower court, printed | `ת"פ (מקומיים י-ם) 2857/85 מדינת ישראל נ' אורנן, פ"מ התשמ"ז(ג) 334 (1987).` |
| Unpublished (Nevo) | `ת"כ (תחרות) 745-07-18 בנק מזרחי טפחות בע"מ נ' הממונה על התחרות (נבו 28.11.2019).` |
| One judge's paragraphs | `בג"ץ 8300/02 נסר נ' ממשלת ישראל, פס' 35–36 לפסק הדין של הנשיאה (בדימ') ביניש (אר"ש 22.5.2012).` |
| Law | `חוק איסור נהיגה ברכב בחוף הים, התשנ"ז–1997, ס"ח 84.` |
| A section of a Basic Law | `ס' 10 לחוק-יסוד: הממשלה, ס"ח התשס"א 158, 159.` |
| Regulations | `תקנות הנמלים (תיקון מס' 3), התשמ"א–1981, ק"ת 956.` |
| Bill | `הצעת חוק ההתיישנות, התשס"ד–2004, ה"ח הממשלה 611.` |
| Book | `אהרן ברק פרשנות במשפט כרך שני: פרשנות החקיקה (1993).` |
| Article | `יפה זילברשץ "על חופש הביטוי המסחרי" משפט וממשל ג 509, חלקים ד(3)-(4) (1996).` |

- A **printed** ruling takes its report (פ"ד, פ"מ), volume, first page and year. Leave the
  report empty for an **unpublished** one, and give the database (נבו, אר"ש) and the date.
- The **Supreme Court** has no court in parentheses; every other court does.
- A **law**: type a date (`1997-03-05`) in the year field and the Hebrew year is filled in
  (התשנ"ז). A Basic Law is cited by its collection year instead.
- **Authors** are full names, separated by commas; Hebrew joins the last one with ו
  (אהרן ברק ובני שגיא).

## From a case number in the note

Put the cursor on a case number such as `ע"א 1234/05`, `בבג״ץ 7/48` or

pages.title: Markdown fidelity
pages.description: How closely Lumen follows the CommonMark and GFM specs, and the promise that opening and saving a file in either editor gives you back the same bytes.
pages.md:
A Markdown editor should never rewrite your files behind your back. Lumen is
tested against the official specs, and against its own round trip: open a
file, save it, and get exactly the bytes you started with.

## Spec conformance

Lumen's parser is tested against the official spec examples, which are kept
in the repository unmodified:

| Suite | Examples | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| CommonMark 0.31.2 | 652 | at least 99% |
| GitHub Flavored Markdown 0.29 | 670 (2 disabled upstream) | at least 98% |

The CommonMark parser underneath (micromark) passes every CommonMark example
on its own. What Lumen adds on top changes a handful of results on purpose:

| Where Lumen differs | Why |
|---|---|
| A leading `---` block is frontmatter | It holds the note's metadata (title, tags). The spec reads it as a thematic break and text. |
| A bare URL or email address becomes a link | GFM autolink literals are always on, including in examples that test plain CommonMark. |
| `ftp://` addresses are not linked automatically | Matches github.com today. Write `<ftp://…>` to link one. |
| Disallowed raw HTML (`<script>`, `<title>`, …) is not filtered by the parser | The preview sanitizes all raw HTML afterwards, which removes these tags. |
| A single line break inside a paragraph shows as a line break | The preview's soft-break setting. It is not part of the gated score. |

The GFM spec is pinned to CommonMark 0.29. Where CommonMark 0.31.2 changed the
expected result for the same input (mostly the emphasis rules), Lumen follows
the newer spec, and those examples are left out of the GFM score.

Any other failing example fails the suite, so every difference has to be
explained here.

## Round trip

Both editors are tested on more than 200 real Markdown files: everything in
the repository, Hebrew documentation included, and every section of the two
spec files. A CRLF copy of every tenth file is added on top.

- **Source editor:** open and save is byte-identical for every file. A file
  with Windows (CRLF) line endings stays CRLF. One with old Mac (CR) endings
  stays CR. In a file with mixed endings, the stray carriage returns stay
  where they are, shown as a special-character mark.
- **WYSIWYG:** unedited blocks are saved exactly as the file had them. An edit
  rewrites only the block you changed, such as the paragraph, list or table
  you typed in. Everything else keeps its own style: `*` or `-` bullets,
  `__bold__` or `**bold**`, table padding and blank lines. Blocks that WYSIWYG
  does not display, such as link reference definitions, are kept in place. A
  CRLF file gets CRLF in the blocks you add.

## Checking it yourself

```sh
npm run md:conformance
```

This runs the conformance suite, the round trip through both editors, and
the unit tests for the source-preserving save. The full results, with every
failing example and a per-file diff of the WYSIWYG serialization, are written
to `test-results/md-conformance/` and `test-results/md-roundtrip/`.

The spec files are © John MacFarlane and GitHub, Inc., under
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Their
source and commit are recorded in `src/__tests__/fixtures/md-spec/README.md`.

pages.title: Messages, empty states and undo
pages.description: How Lumen talks when something fails, when a panel is empty, and before it deletes anything — and the guide for writing those messages.
pages.md:
Lumen holds three promises about the moments people notice most:

1. **An error says what happened, what is safe, and what to do** — never a
   stack trace, an error code or a library's own words.
2. **An empty panel shows the way out**: one short sentence and one action.
3. **Nothing you made is deleted without a way back**: the action can be
   undone, or it asks first.

## Errors

Every error shown in the app goes through `explainError(e)`
(`src/lib/userError.ts`). It recognises the kind of failure and shows one
sentence for it, in the user's language; the raw text goes to the log, where
the AI doctor and a bug report can read it.

| Kind | What the person reads |
|---|---|
| no space | This device is out of storage space. Your text is still open here; free some space or export the vault, then try again. |
| permission | The browser did not allow this. Nothing was changed; allow access when it asks, then try again. |
| network | No connection. Your notes are safe on this device; try again when you are online. |
| timeout | This took too long and was stopped. Nothing was lost; try again, or try a smaller piece. |
| not found | The file is no longer there (moved or deleted). Nothing else changed; look for it in the trash or reopen it. |
| damaged file | The file could not be read: it is damaged or in another format. Nothing was changed; check the file and try again. |
| name taken | Something with that name is already there. Nothing was overwritten; choose another name. |
| AI busy | The AI service is busy (too many requests). Nothing was lost; wait a minute and try again. |
| no AI key, privacy policy, no local model | what was (not) sent, and where to change it |
| anything else | Something went wrong. Nothing you wrote is lost; try again, and if it happens again, the AI doctor and the log have the details. |

A cancel the person did themselves (closing a file picker, pressing Stop)
shows nothing. An error whose words are already written for the person
(translated, with what to do) is thrown as a `UserFacingError` and shown as
it is.

One exception is allowed: the syntax error of the person's **own** code or
diagram (Mermaid, Graphviz, PlantUML, ABC, SQL, a database block's query),
because its line and token are what they need to fix it. Each one is marked
`raw-error-allow` in the code.

## Writing a message (the guide)

- **What happened** — in the person's terms, not the program's: "The file
  could not be read", not "SyntaxError: Unexpected token".
- **What is safe** — say what did not happen: "Nothing was changed", "Your
  text is still open here", "Nothing was sent".
- **What to do** — one concrete next step: "free some space", "try again when
  you are online", "add a key in AI settings".
- No blame ("you entered an invalid…"), no codes, no exclamation marks, no
  "Oops". One or two short sentences.
- In Hebrew: plural address (נסו, בחרו) as in the rest of the app; the verb
  first ("שום דבר לא השתנה"); product and format names stay in Latin script
  (Ollama, WebGPU, ‎.zip).

## Empty states

Every empty panel — the file tree, search, outline, backlinks, tags,
comments, the graph, the trash, version history, templates, the audit log,
the privacy ledger, the AI panels — is an `` with one action:
*New note*, *Clear the search*, *Add a heading*, *Copy a link to this note*,
*Keep a version now*, and so on. The component's `action` is required.

## Destructive actions

Moving a note to the trash offers **Undo**; deleting from the trash for good,
emptying the trash, clearing the agent runs, deleting a comment, removing the
Hebrew dictionary, a git pull (which replaces files — and now moves files
deleted upstream to the trash instead of deleting them), applying the Vault
Doctor's link fixes and clearing the style profile **ask first**. A command
that deletes or replaces data declares `destructive: "confirm" | "undo"`.

## How it is checked

Three gates run in the unit tests (`src/__tests__/respectfulMessages.test.ts`)
and can be run alone:

```sh
node scripts/check-raw-errors.mjs     # 0 raw error texts on screen
node scripts/check-empty-states.mjs   # every empty state has an action
node scripts/check-destructive.mjs    # every destructive action asks or can be undone
```

pages.description: Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG — pick the one that fits the task.
pages.md:
Lumen has four editor surfaces. Switch with `⌘1` / `⌘2` / `⌘3` / `⌘4`.

## Source (`⌘1`)

Plain CodeMirror 6 with markdown highlighting. Use it when you want to
write fast, see exactly what the file contains, or paste pre-formatted
markdown. The "Smart Insert" pill (`⌘⇧V`) is most powerful here.

**Best for**: writers who think in markdown; data-heavy notes where you
want the fence delimiters visible.

## Split (`⌘2`, default)

Editor on one side, live preview on the other. The split orientation
follows your viewport — horizontal on wide screens, vertical on phones.
Override via the **Scroll orientation** menu in the top bar.

Scroll-link is on by default — both panes track the same heading even at
different content heights.

**Best for**: most authoring sessions. You see the rendered output the
moment you type.

## Preview (`⌘3`)

Read-only render of the markdown. Tables, charts, diagrams, math, embeds
— everything in its final form. Print from here with
`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`, which keeps the colours so PDFs come out
faithful.

**Best for**: reading notes back, proof-reading, sharing your screen.

## WYSIWYG (`⌘4`)

Notion-grade editing on top of Milkdown / ProseMirror. Slash menu (`/`),
inline math, drag-and-drop block reordering. Round-trips to plain
markdown — so a doc you wrote in WYSIWYG opens cleanly in Source.

**Best for**: visual thinkers; rich documents (presentations, decks);
anyone migrating from Notion.

## Toggle without leaving the keyboard

| Key | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘1` | Source |
| `⌘2` | Split |
| `⌘3` | Preview |
| `⌘4` | WYSIWYG |

The mode is remembered across reloads, so you come back to the view you
last used.

## Suggesting mode (track changes)

Turn it on from the command palette ("Turn on suggesting mode (track changes)") or with
the **Editing / Suggesting** pill in the status bar. While it is on, edits
in the Source / Split editor and in WYSIWYG are recorded as
[CriticMarkup](https://github.com/CriticMarkup/CriticMarkup-toolkit), so
the file stays plain markdown:

| You do | Stored as |
| --- | --- |
| Type text | `{++inserted++}` |
| Delete text (Backspace, Delete, cut) | `{--deleted--}` |
| Type over a selection | `{~~old~>new~~}` |
| Write a note by hand | `{>>comment<<}` / `{==highlight==}` |

- Typing next to your own insertion extends it, and consecutive deletions
  merge. Deleting text inside your own `{++ ++}` really deletes it.
- Undo / redo, edits from collaborators, and edits inside code blocks or
  inline code are never turned into suggestions.
- The editor shows insertions underlined in green, deletions struck
  through in red and comments highlighted; the preview renders them as
  `<ins>`, `<del>` and `<mark>`.
- Palette commands: accept / reject the suggestion at the cursor, accept
  all, reject all, next / previous suggestion. All of them work in
  WYSIWYG too; accept all / reject all also work from Preview.
- **In WYSIWYG** suggestions show as underlined insertions and struck-out
  deletions (hover for the author). Typing is recorded as an insertion,
  Backspace / Delete leave the text struck out and step over it, and
  typing over a selection becomes a substitution. Structural edits —
  joining two paragraphs with Backspace — aren't recorded as a
  suggestion and are undone; turn suggesting off for those.
- The status-bar pill shows how many suggestions the document contains.
- **Who suggested it.** When you are signed in, each new suggestion is
  followed by an author tag — a comment holding only `@name`, e.g.
  `{++new text++}{>>@Tal<<}`. The tag belongs to its change: accepting
  or rejecting the change removes it too. Hover a suggestion to see
  "Suggested by …"; the preview shows the name as a small comment.
  Typing inside someone else's suggestion keeps their name on it.

## TypeScript checks in code blocks

Run **Enable TypeScript checks in code blocks** from the command palette.
In the Source / Split editor, every ` ```ts `, ` ```typescript ` and
` ```tsx ` block (and JavaScript blocks, see below) is then checked by the
real TypeScript compiler:

- Errors get a wavy underline — hover it for the message (`TS2322: …`).
- Hovering a name shows its type (and its JSDoc, if any).
- Completions pop up while you type (after `.` or a few letters;
  `Ctrl-Space` forces them).
- Each block is checked on its own (its declarations don't leak into
  other blocks), in strict mode against the ES2022 and DOM libraries.
  Imports of npm packages aren't resolved and aren't reported.
- JavaScript blocks (` ```js `, ` ```javascript `, ` ```live-js `) get
  syntax errors, hover and completions; add `// @ts-check` as the first
  line to also get type errors.
- ` ```live-js shared ` blocks are checked together per scope
  (`shared=name`), in document order — a later block sees the names an
  earlier one declared, exactly as when they run. Re-declaring a name
  there is allowed.

The compiler (~1.3 MB compressed) runs in a background worker and is
downloaded only after you turn the setting on; it is not part of the
offline app shell. The setting is remembered.

pages.description: Callouts, comments, coloured highlights, footnotes with hover, math and image sizes, written the way Obsidian writes them, so a vault moves to Lumen without changing a line.
pages.md:
A vault that comes from Obsidian uses this syntax every day. Lumen reads it,
shows it in the preview and both editors, and saves it back without
changing it.

## Callouts

```md
> [!warning] Mind the gap
> The platform is curved.

> [!faq]- A question that starts folded
> Click the title to open it.
```

- Every Obsidian type works: `note`, `abstract`, `info`, `todo`, `tip`,
  `success`, `question`, `warning`, `failure`, `danger`, `bug`, `example`
  and `quote`, plus their aliases (`summary`, `hint`, `check`, `faq`,
  `caution`, `error`, `cite`, …). An unknown type looks like a note.
- `+` after the type makes the callout foldable and open, and `-` makes it
  foldable and closed.
- Without a title, the callout shows its type in your language.
- A Hebrew callout reads right to left, with its colour bar on the right.
- Callouts can be nested.

## Comments

`%%like this%%` is hidden in the preview, inline or across several
paragraphs. An unclosed `%%` hides the rest of the note, as in Obsidian.
The editors show comments faded, so you can still edit them.

## Highlights

`==text==` is highlighted. A colour emoji at the start picks the colour
(Obsidian 1.14): `==🔴urgent==`, and also 🟠 🟡 🟢 🔵 🟣. Highlights can
contain bold, italics and links, and they also work in table cells and
in Hebrew.

## Footnotes

`Text[^1]` with `[^1]: The note.` anywhere in the file. Hovering over or
tabbing to the number shows the footnote next to it, without scrolling to
the end of the note. Escape closes it.

## Math

`$inline$` and `$$block$$` math. The math renderer loads only when a note
contains math, so it never slows down opening the app.

## Images and their size

| Written | Shows |
|---|---|
| `![[photo.png]]` | the image |
| `![[photo.png\|300]]` | 300 pixels wide |
| `![[photo.png\|640x360]]` | 640 × 360 |
| `![[photo.png\|A cat\|200]]` | with alt text, 200 wide |
| `![A cat\|200](photo.png)` | the Markdown form, 200 wide |

In the preview, drag an image's edge (the right edge in English, the left
in Hebrew) to resize it. The new width is written into the note, as in
Obsidian 1.12.

## Tested

Forty golden notes covering all of the above, in English and Hebrew, are
rendered on every test run and checked element by element. They are also
part of the [round-trip corpus](/editor/markdown-fidelity/), so both editors
must save them byte for byte.
